## Highlights

In 2024, total environmental tax revenue in the EU amounted to €371.9 billion, representing 2.1% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) and 5.1% of total EU government revenue from taxes and social contributions (TSC).

Taxes on energy in the EU accounted for more than three-quarters of the total revenues from environmental taxes (77.2% of the total) in 2024, well ahead of taxes on transport (18.0%) and pollution and resources (4.8%).

[![Image 3: Vertical stacked bar chart showing environmental tax revenue by type in euro billions for the EU. Each year column contains three stacks representing energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resources taxes, all in euro billions. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/5/5a/Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg/700px-Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg)

_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

This article provides an updated overview of [environmental tax](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Environmental_tax "Glossary:Environmental tax") data in the [European Union (EU)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Union_(EU) "Glossary:European Union (EU)"), incorporating the latest figures up to 2024. According to [Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:02011R0691-20140616:EN:NOT), an environmental tax is a tax whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific negative impact on the environment and which is defined in the [European system of accounts](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_system_of_national_and_regional_accounts_(ESA_2010) "Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)") (ESA 2010) as a tax. The article highlights recent trends in environmental tax revenue statistics and identifies the main contributors to these changes. It also serves as a complement to the existing Eurostat publication on environmentally related taxes '[Environmental Taxes – A Statistical Guide, 2024 edition](http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-GQ-23-016&language=en)'.

## Environmental taxes in the EU

The €371.9 billion in environmental taxes recorded for the EU in 2024 represents a 6.1% increase compared with 2023, following a 3.8% increase between 2022 and 2023. Despite these increases, the share of environmental taxes in [total tax](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Tax_revenue "Glossary:Tax revenue") and [social contribution](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Social_contributions "Glossary:Social contributions") revenues, excluding [imputed social contributions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions "Glossary:Imputed social contributions"), declined from 6.1% in 2021 to 5.2% in 2024, a decrease of 0.9 [percentage points (pp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Percentage_point "Glossary:Percentage point") (see Figure 1 below). This indicates that, although environmental tax revenues continued to increase in absolute terms, they grew more slowly than overall tax and social contribution revenues.

[![Image 4: Combined vertical stacked bar and line chart showing environmental tax revenue by type and total environmental taxes as a share of TSC and GDP in the EU from 2014 to 2024. Energy taxes are the largest component of environmental tax revenue throughout the period. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/a/a7/SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png)

Figure 1: Environmental tax revenue by type and total environmental taxes as share of TSC (total government revenue from taxes and social contributions) and GDP (gross domestic product), EU 2014-2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, environmental taxes accounted for 5.2% of total revenues from taxes and social contributions in the EU, continuing the slight decline observed since 2021 (6.1%). Considerable differences remained across countries.

Bulgaria (9.7%) and Greece (9.4%) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial decreases over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7%), Slovenia (7.3%), Latvia (7.2%), and Poland (7.0%). At the other end of the scale, Luxembourg recorded the lowest share (2.9%), followed by Sweden (3.9%) and Norway (4.0%). While most countries showed only modest year-to-year changes, notable increases were observed in Italy, where the share rose from 5.5% in 2022 to 6.5% in 2024, and in Hungary from 5.2% in 2022 to 5.8% in 2024. Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe.

[![Image 5: Vertical bar chart showing Environmental taxes for 2022, 2023, and 2024 as a percentage of total revenues from taxes and social contributions. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/8/83/SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png)

Figure 2: Environmental taxes, as percentage of total taxes and social contributions (but excluding [imputed social contributions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions "Glossary:Imputed social contributions")) for 2022, 2023, and 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

## Environmental tax categories

**Environmental energy taxes remain the main source of revenues in most countries**

Environmental tax revenue is divided into four main categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, pollution taxes, and resource taxes. Given the relatively small share of pollution and resource taxes in total environmental tax revenue, along with difficulties in classifying some minor national taxes, this article combines these two categories when presenting the breakdown of environmental taxes.

In 2024, total environmental tax revenue across the EU amounted to approximately €371.9 billion, with energy taxes constituting the largest share at €287.0 billion, followed by transport taxes at €67.0 billion, and pollution and resource taxes combined accounting for €17.9 billion.

[![Image 6: Table showing total environmental tax revenue by type of tax and tax payer as percentages and euro millions in the EU for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/d/df/SE-ETEA26-Table1.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Table1.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Table1.png)

Table 1: Total environmental tax revenue by type of tax (including and excluding [imputed social contributions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions "Glossary:Imputed social contributions")) and tax payer, EU 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en), [(gov_10a_taxag)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10a_taxag/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, environmental tax revenue in the EU was composed mainly of energy taxes, which accounted for more than 77.2% of the EU’s environmental tax revenue (totalling approximately €287.0 billion). This category encompasses [levies](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Levies "Glossary:Levies") on energy products such as coal, oil products, natural gas, and [electricity](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Electricity "Glossary:Electricity") used for both stationary and transport purposes. By convention, CO₂ taxes are also included within this group.

Transport taxes formed the second-largest category, generating approximately €67.0 billion, representing around 18.0% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. These taxes primarily consist of levies related to motor vehicle ownership and usage.

Meanwhile, pollution and resources taxes made up the smallest share, generating approximately €17.9 billion and accounting for about 4.8% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. Pollution and resource taxes include various types of taxes on [raw material](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Raw_material "Glossary:Raw material") extraction, air and water emissions, noise, and waste management.

Figure 3 shows environmental tax revenues in 2024 as a percentage of [GDP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:GDP "Glossary:GDP") and of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions, excluding imputed social contributions. The latter is further broken down into energy, transport, and pollution and resource taxes. Comparable data are also available for three EFTA countries.

In the EU, energy taxes accounted for the largest share of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions (4.04%), followed by transport taxes (0.94%), and pollution and resource taxes (0.25%). Among the Member States, the contribution of energy taxes ranged from 2.35% in Malta to 8.89% in Bulgaria, while transport taxes ranged from 0.06% in Czechia to 2.04% in the Netherlands. Pollution and resource taxes generally represented only a small proportion of total government revenue, although relatively high values were observed in Croatia (1.58%) and the Netherlands (1.10%). Overall environmental tax revenues amounted to 2.06% of GDP in the EU, ranging from 0.97% in Ireland to 3.76% in Greece.

Among the [EFTA](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:EFTA "Glossary:EFTA") countries, Switzerland recorded the highest contribution from transport taxes (2.24%), while Iceland stood out for its comparatively low contribution from energy taxes (1.55%) and relatively high contribution from pollution and resource taxes (1.07%). Environmental tax revenues amounted to 1.44% of GDP in Switzerland, 1.58% in Norway, and 1.56% in Iceland.

[![Image 7: Stacked vertical bar chart showing environmental tax revenue in 2024 for EU countries and Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland as a percentage of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions (TSC), with a circle marker on each bar indicating the same revenue as a percentage of GDP. Each country’s bar is split into three categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resource taxes. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/2/23/SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png)

Figure 3: Environmental tax revenue by category as% of TSC (total government revenue from taxes and social contributions) and GDP, 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en), [(gov_10a_taxag)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10a_taxag/default/table?lang=en)

**Environmental tax revenue by payer and NACE**

In 2024, the 6.1% growth in environmental tax revenues (see Figure 4) differed considerably across institutional sectors and countries, with the largest variations observed for corporations.

At EU level, the contribution of corporations to the growth of environmental tax revenues was 2.8%. Several countries recorded a particularly strong contribution from corporations to tax revenues growth, notably Romania (+19.2%), Hungary (+14.8%), Latvia (+13.2%), Poland (+10.6%) and Lithuania (+8.2%). In contrast, corporations made a negative contribution to the growth of environmental tax revenues in Sweden (-18.5%), Luxembourg (-6.8%), Greece (-4.5%), Bulgaria (-3.9%), Germany and Slovakia (both -2.0%), and Finland (-1.1%).

Contributions to the growth of tax revenues by households were generally more moderate, with a positive contribution in most countries and with a negative contribution in a limited number of Member States. Contributions to growth by non-residents remained close to zero in almost all countries and had little impact on overall developments. Overall, the results indicate that changes in environmental tax revenues in 2024 were driven primarily by developments in the corporate sector rather than by households.

[![Image 8: Stacked column chart showing the growth of environmental tax revenues from 2023 to 2024 for the EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland and Iceland, and candidate countries, decomposed into contributions from households, corporations, and non-residents. EU environmental tax revenues increased by around 6%, mainly due to corporations. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/4/4a/SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png)

Figure 4: Growth in environmental taxes 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en)

To succeed in the [EU's climate neutrality objective by 2050](https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/climate-strategies-targets/2050-long-term-strategy_en), taxation systems are a key policy tool. Well-designed tax reforms can stimulate economic growth, reduce [greenhouse gas](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG) "Glossary:Greenhouse gas (GHG)") emissions through effective carbon pricing, and support an equitable transition.

In 2024, total environmental tax revenues are almost evenly split between households and the corporations sector. The donut chart below (Figure 5) shows the distribution of environmental tax revenues in the EU for the year 2024, categorised by payer type: Households, Non-Residents, and Corporations (classified under [NACE](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:NACE "Glossary:NACE"), which is the classification used for economic activities).

Environmental taxes paid by households accounted for 47.5% of total environmental tax revenues, while corporations contributed 50.5% to total environmental taxes. Among corporations, those active in manufacturing activities (NACE C) contributed the most, accounting for 11.6% of total environmental taxes; corporations in transport and storage activities (NACE H) followed, contributing 10.1%. Non-residents paid 2.0% of total environmental taxes.

[![Image 9: Doughnut chart showing the breakdown of environmental tax revenue in the EU in 2024 by payer. Industries (NACE) account for 50.5% of total environmental tax revenue, households for 47.5%, and non-residents for 2.0%.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/0/0a/SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png)

Figure 5: Contributions to environmental tax revenue 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

Although in 2024 environmental tax revenues in the EU were nearly evenly split between households and corporations, national patterns vary significantly (see Figure 6 below).

Some countries like Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, and France rely heavily on household contributions (over 55%), while Romania, Estonia, Czechia, and Bulgaria show a strong industrial tax contribution. Luxembourg stands out with more than one third (35.8%) of its environmental tax revenue coming from non-residents, likely due to cross-border fuel sales. In contrast, countries such as Germany, Cyprus, and Sweden display a more balanced distribution across payer groups. These variations reflect national economic structures, energy use, and policy choices affecting environmental taxation.

## Energy taxes

**Energy taxes: corporations surpass households as primary contributors**

Energy taxes are the primary source of environmental tax revenues in the EU, which is a trend that continued in 2024 for all different payer groups. In the EU, households contributed an average of 43.3% to energy taxes, underlining their key role in final energy consumption (see Figure 8).

**Emission permits**

EU Member States generate substantial revenue through emission permits, which allow holders to release a specific amount of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Under the European [Emissions Trading System (ETS)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Emissions_trading_system_(ETS) "Glossary:Emissions trading system (ETS)"), these permits are classified as taxes according to ESA 2010, the standard used for compiling macroeconomic statistics, including National Accounts. Governments are increasingly using cap-and-trade schemes like the EU ETS to regulate CO2 emissions. Launched in 2005, the EU ETS initially allocated emission allowances for free. Since 2013, however, auctioning has become the primary method for distributing these permits. In the third phase of the ETS (2013–2020), over 70% of allowances were auctioned, and this figure has continued to rise, with phase 4 (2021–2030) introducing a gradual reduction in the total number of emission permits. This phase focuses on protecting sectors at risk of relocating production outside the EU by providing 100% free permits, while free allocations for less exposed sectors will be phased out after 2026. Revenue from ETS auctions is recorded as "other taxes on production" (D.29) under ESA 2010. This means the revenue is recognised in the year the permits are used for emissions, rather than when they are auctioned.

In 2024, EU countries reported €31.3 billion in revenues from EU emissions trading system (ETS) allowances (see Figure 9), representing a 3.5% decrease compared with 2023. Between 2014 and 2024, the marked growth, particularly after 2017, reflects strengthening carbon pricing and the expanding role of emissions trading.

In 2024, Poland (€5.7 billion) and Germany (€5.5 billion) were the largest contributors, while Spain and Italy each reported revenues exceeding €3 billion. Although revenues from ETS allowances declined in Hungary and Luxembourg, most Member States recorded increases. In total the EU aggregate increased by 3.5% in 2024. Overall, the data underline the continued importance of the EU ETS as a key instrument for carbon pricing across the European Union.

## Transport taxes

**Transport taxes: households shoulder the majority of the burden**

This category covers taxes on energy production and on energy products used for both transportation and stationary applications. Key transport fuels include petrol and diesel, while energy sources for stationary use comprise fuel oils, natural gas, coal, and electricity. Taxes on [biofuels](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Biofuels "Glossary:Biofuels") and other [renewable energy sources](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources "Glossary:Renewable energy sources") are also included, as well as taxes on energy product stockpiles. Transport taxes, typically applied to vehicle purchases and road usage, have tended to fluctuate in line with vehicle sales.

In 2024, transport tax revenues in the EU amounted to €67.0 billion, of which €44.6 billion (66.6%) were paid by households, €21.7 billion (32.4%) by industries, and €0.7 billion (1.1%) by non-residents (see Figure 10). Compared with 2023, transport tax revenue increased for all payer groups, with the largest relative increase recorded in taxes paid by non-residents (+13.9%), although these represented only a small share of total transport tax revenue. Households remained the principal contributors to transport tax revenues throughout the EU.

[![Image 14: Stacked vertical bar chart showing transport taxes by economic activity as percentage of transport tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/2/2c/SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png)

_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, households were by far the main contributors to transport tax revenues in the EU, accounting for 66.6% on average. This reflects the strong link between transport taxes and private vehicle ownership and use. Transport taxes include, in particular, vehicle registration taxes and other related taxes. The services sector followed with 23.1%, while industry (8.2%), agriculture (1.1%), and non-residents (1.1%) made up smaller shares.

National patterns vary widely: Ireland (80.4%), Malta (78.7%), and Finland (76.2%) show particularly high household shares, indicating a tax structure focused on private vehicle users. In contrast, Slovakia (11.4%) and Czechia (11.5%) report much lower household shares, with the bulk of transport taxes paid by businesses, especially in the services sector, which contributes over 55% in both countries. These differences reflect national transport habits, tax policies, and vehicle ownership trends across Europe.

## Pollution and resource taxes

**Pollution and resource taxes: data indicate a diverse approach across the EU**

For 2024, pollution and resource taxes remain the smallest category with a consistent upward trend (see Figure 11). Starting at about €10 billion in 2008, they increased to around €17.9 billion in 2024. This reflects a growing recognition of the need to address broader environmental issues, not just energy and transportation, but the more extensive impact of resource use and pollution.

In 2024, pollution and resource tax revenues in the EU were mainly paid by households (44.1%), followed by industries (31.5%), and the services sector (18.8%). The share from agriculture remained relatively small, averaging 2.8%, while non-residents contributed 2.0%. The distribution of these taxes reflects the varying ways countries apply environmental taxes and levies, with some focusing more on household-level waste and pollution charges, and others on industrial emissions or resource use. Overall, the data indicates a diverse approach across the EU to taxing environmental impacts beyond energy and transport.

## Conclusion

Environmental taxes should not be interpreted independently of other environmental accounts—they are embedded within the broader framework of monetary environmental accounts and closely linked to related statistical areas such as Environmental Protection Expenditure Accounts (EPEA), Environmental Subsidies and Similar Transfers (ESST), and potentially environmentally damaging subsidies (PEDS). At the same time, analysing environmental tax revenues alongside other datasets—such as [air emission accounts](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Air_emissions_accounts_(AEA) "Glossary:Air emissions accounts (AEA)") or energy balances—provides valuable insights into the interactions between economic instruments and environmental pressures. This integrated perspective supports more comprehensive and effective policy analysis and decision-making.

## Data sources

Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes at a detailed level, by economic activity, under [Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/691/oj/eng) on European environmental economic accounts. The Eurostat publication titled '[Environmental taxes — a statistical guide](http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-GQ-23-016&language=en)' constitutes the methodological basis for this data collection. In addition, using 'National Tax Lists', a supporting dataset to Table 9 from the ESA transmission programme, Eurostat gathers data on environmental taxes for 3 categories: energy, transport, and pollution/resource taxes. The data are then validated and published.

Data relating to environmental taxes can be used to analyse the revenue stream from such taxes and to provide a relative measure of the importance of these taxes through the calculation of ratios relative to GDP or to the total revenue from all taxes and social contributions. In the first case (ratio relative to GDP), the comparison helps to provide an understanding of the tax burden. In the second case, the comparison helps to assess whether or not the tax burden is shifting from other tax bases (for example, labour income) towards environmental taxes. It has to be noted that the total revenue of taxes and social contributions used to compute the ratio does not include imputed social contributions. For further information concerning various tax aggregates, see ['Main national accounts tax aggregates'](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/974dcfe2-4a39-4870-b8a3-70d58f56ff79?lang=en).

Environmental tax revenue can also be allocated according to the different economic activities paying the taxes. Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes using a categorisation by economic activity (based on the [NACE Rev. 2](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE) "Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)") classification supplemented by information for households, non-residents, and a residual category for taxes that could not be allocated).

Increasing revenue from environmental taxes should be interpreted with caution. The increases may be caused by the introduction of new taxes or an increase in tax rates, or alternatively may be linked to an increase in the tax base caused, for instance, by a higher consumption of energy products.

## Context

In today’s economy, production and consumption decisions have a significant impact on the environment. Environmental policies, in particular fiscal policies through taxes, seek to balance economic growth with ecological sustainability. These environmentally related taxes are based on the ‘polluter-pays’ principle, encouraging more sustainable behaviour while generating revenue to address environmental damage. Environmental taxes are an important policy instrument in the EU’s strategic agenda, aimed at strengthening its competitiveness and ensuring the success of the climate neutrality objective.

Economic instruments for pollution control and natural resource management are an important part of environmental policy in the EU Member States. The range of instruments that are available includes, among others, environmental taxes, fees and charges, tradeable permits, deposit-refund systems, and [subsidies](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Subsidies "Glossary:Subsidies").

The [European Green Deal](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640) creates the context for well-designed tax reforms which boost economic growth and resilience to climate shocks and help contribute to a fairer society and to a just transition. Environmental taxes play a direct role by sending the right price signals and providing the right incentives for sustainable behaviour by producers, users, and consumers.

The use of economic tools for the benefit of the environment is also promoted in Goal 17 of the [EU sustainable development goals](http://ec.europa.eu/environment/sustainable-development/SDGs/implementation/index_en.htm).

## Highlights

In 2024, total environmental tax revenue in the EU amounted to €371.9 billion, representing 2.1% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) and 5.1% of total EU government revenue from taxes and social contributions (TSC).

Taxes on energy in the EU accounted for more than three-quarters of the total revenues from environmental taxes (77.2% of the total) in 2024, well ahead of taxes on transport (18.0%) and pollution and resources (4.8%).

[![Image 3: Vertical stacked bar chart showing environmental tax revenue by type in euro billions for the EU. Each year column contains three stacks representing energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resources taxes, all in euro billions. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/5/5a/Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg/700px-Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg)

_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

This article provides an updated overview of [environmental tax](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Environmental_tax "Glossary:Environmental tax") data in the [European Union (EU)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Union_(EU) "Glossary:European Union (EU)"), incorporating the latest figures up to 2024. According to [Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:02011R0691-20140616:EN:NOT), an environmental tax is a tax whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific negative impact on the environment and which is defined in the [European system of accounts](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_system_of_national_and_regional_accounts_(ESA_2010) "Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)") (ESA 2010) as a tax. The article highlights recent trends in environmental tax revenue statistics and identifies the main contributors to these changes. It also serves as a complement to the existing Eurostat publication on environmentally related taxes '[Environmental Taxes – A Statistical Guide, 2024 edition](http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-GQ-23-016&language=en)'.

## Environmental taxes in the EU

The €371.9 billion in environmental taxes recorded for the EU in 2024 represents a 6.1% increase compared with 2023, following a 3.8% increase between 2022 and 2023. Despite these increases, the share of environmental taxes in [total tax](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Tax_revenue "Glossary:Tax revenue") and [social contribution](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Social_contributions "Glossary:Social contributions") revenues, excluding [imputed social contributions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions "Glossary:Imputed social contributions"), declined from 6.1% in 2021 to 5.2% in 2024, a decrease of 0.9 [percentage points (pp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Percentage_point "Glossary:Percentage point") (see Figure 1 below). This indicates that, although environmental tax revenues continued to increase in absolute terms, they grew more slowly than overall tax and social contribution revenues.

[![Image 4: Combined vertical stacked bar and line chart showing environmental tax revenue by type and total environmental taxes as a share of TSC and GDP in the EU from 2014 to 2024. Energy taxes are the largest component of environmental tax revenue throughout the period. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/a/a7/SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png)

_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, environmental taxes accounted for 5.2% of total revenues from taxes and social contributions in the EU, continuing the slight decline observed since 2021 (6.1%). Considerable differences remained across countries.

Bulgaria (9.7%) and Greece (9.4%) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial decreases over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7%), Slovenia (7.3%), Latvia (7.2%), and Poland (7.0%). At the other end of the scale, Luxembourg recorded the lowest share (2.9%), followed by Sweden (3.9%) and Norway (4.0%). While most countries showed only modest year-to-year changes, notable increases were observed in Italy, where the share rose from 5.5% in 2022 to 6.5% in 2024, and in Hungary from 5.2% in 2022 to 5.8% in 2024. Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe.

For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/8/83/SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png)

## Environmental tax categories

**Environmental energy taxes remain the main source of revenues in most countries**

Environmental tax revenue is divided into four main categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, pollution taxes, and resource taxes. Given the relatively small share of pollution and resource taxes in total environmental tax revenue, along with difficulties in classifying some minor national taxes, this article combines these two categories when presenting the breakdown of environmental taxes.

In 2024, total environmental tax revenue across the EU amounted to approximately €371.9 billion, with energy taxes constituting the largest share at €287.0 billion, followed by transport taxes at €67.0 billion, and pollution and resource taxes combined accounting for €17.9 billion.

[![Image 6: Table showing total environmental tax revenue by type of tax and tax payer as percentages and euro millions in the EU for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/d/df/SE-ETEA26-Table1.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Table1.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Table1.png)

Table 1: Total environmental tax revenue by type of tax (including and excluding [imputed social contributions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions "Glossary:Imputed social contributions")) and tax payer, EU 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(nama_10_gdp)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en), [(gov_10a_taxag)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10a_taxag/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, environmental tax revenue in the EU was composed mainly of energy taxes, which accounted for more than 77.2% of the EU’s environmental tax revenue (totalling approximately €287.0 billion). This category encompasses [levies](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Levies "Glossary:Levies") on energy products such as coal, oil products, natural gas, and [electricity](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Electricity "Glossary:Electricity") used for both stationary and transport purposes. By convention, CO₂ taxes are also included within this group.

Transport taxes formed the second-largest category, generating approximately €67.0 billion, representing around 18.0% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. These taxes primarily consist of levies related to motor vehicle ownership and usage.

Meanwhile, pollution and resources taxes made up the smallest share, generating approximately €17.9 billion and accounting for about 4.8% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. Pollution and resource taxes include various types of taxes on [raw material](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Raw_material "Glossary:Raw material") extraction, air and water emissions, noise, and waste management.

Figure 3 shows environmental tax revenues in 2024 as a percentage of [GDP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:GDP "Glossary:GDP") and of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions, excluding imputed social contributions. The latter is further broken down into energy, transport, and pollution and resource taxes. Comparable data are also available for three EFTA countries.

In the EU, energy taxes accounted for the largest share of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions (4.04%), followed by transport taxes (0.94%), and pollution and resource taxes (0.25%). Among the Member States, the contribution of energy taxes ranged from 2.35% in Malta to 8.89% in Bulgaria, while transport taxes ranged from 0.06% in Czechia to 2.04% in the Netherlands. Pollution and resource taxes generally represented only a small proportion of total government revenue, although relatively high values were observed in Croatia (1.58%) and the Netherlands (1.10%). Overall environmental tax revenues amounted to 2.06% of GDP in the EU, ranging from 0.97% in Ireland to 3.76% in Greece.

Among the [EFTA](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:EFTA "Glossary:EFTA") countries, Switzerland recorded the highest contribution from transport taxes (2.24%), while Iceland stood out for its comparatively low contribution from energy taxes (1.55%) and relatively high contribution from pollution and resource taxes (1.07%). Environmental tax revenues amounted to 1.44% of GDP in Switzerland, 1.58% in Norway, and 1.56% in Iceland.

Each country’s bar is split into three categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resource taxes. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/2/23/SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png)

**Environmental tax revenue by payer and NACE**

In 2024, the 6.1% growth in environmental tax revenues (see Figure 4) differed considerably across institutional sectors and countries, with the largest variations observed for corporations.

At EU level, the contribution of corporations to the growth of environmental tax revenues was 2.8%. Several countries recorded a particularly strong contribution from corporations to tax revenues growth, notably Romania (+19.2%), Hungary (+14.8%), Latvia (+13.2%), Poland (+10.6%) and Lithuania (+8.2%). In contrast, corporations made a negative contribution to the growth of environmental tax revenues in Sweden (-18.5%), Luxembourg (-6.8%), Greece (-4.5%), Bulgaria (-3.9%), Germany and Slovakia (both -2.0%), and Finland (-1.1%).

Contributions to the growth of tax revenues by households were generally more moderate, with a positive contribution in most countries and with a negative contribution in a limited number of Member States. Contributions to growth by non-residents remained close to zero in almost all countries and had little impact on overall developments. Overall, the results indicate that changes in environmental tax revenues in 2024 were driven primarily by developments in the corporate sector rather than by households.

[![Image 8: Stacked column chart showing the growth of environmental tax revenues from 2023 to 2024 for the EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland and Iceland, and candidate countries, decomposed into contributions from households, corporations, and non-residents. EU environmental tax revenues increased by around 6%, mainly due to corporations. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/4/4a/SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png)

To succeed in the [EU's climate neutrality objective by 2050](https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/climate-strategies-targets/2050-long-term-strategy_en), taxation systems are a key policy tool. Well-designed tax reforms can stimulate economic growth, reduce [greenhouse gas](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG) "Glossary:Greenhouse gas (GHG)") emissions through effective carbon pricing, and support an equitable transition.

In 2024, total environmental tax revenues are almost evenly split between households and the corporations sector. The donut chart below (Figure 5) shows the distribution of environmental tax revenues in the EU for the year 2024, categorised by payer type: Households, Non-Residents, and Corporations (classified under [NACE](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:NACE "Glossary:NACE"), which is the classification used for economic activities).

Environmental taxes paid by households accounted for 47.5% of total environmental tax revenues, while corporations contributed 50.5% to total environmental taxes. Among corporations, those active in manufacturing activities (NACE C) contributed the most, accounting for 11.6% of total environmental taxes; corporations in transport and storage activities (NACE H) followed, contributing 10.1%. Non-residents paid 2.0% of total environmental taxes.

[![Image 9: Doughnut chart showing the breakdown of environmental tax revenue in the EU in 2024 by payer. Industries (NACE) account for 50.5% of total environmental tax revenue, households for 47.5%, and non-residents for 2.0%.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/0/0a/SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png)

Figure 5: Contributions to environmental tax revenue 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

Although in 2024 environmental tax revenues in the EU were nearly evenly split between households and corporations, national patterns vary significantly (see Figure 6 below).

Some countries like Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, and France rely heavily on household contributions (over 55%), while Romania, Estonia, Czechia, and Bulgaria show a strong industrial tax contribution. Luxembourg stands out with more than one third (35.8%) of its environmental tax revenue coming from non-residents, likely due to cross-border fuel sales. In contrast, countries such as Germany, Cyprus, and Sweden display a more balanced distribution across payer groups. These variations reflect national economic structures, energy use, and policy choices affecting environmental taxation.

**Environmental tax revenues fall while labour taxes remain stable**

The [Roadmap to a Resource Efficient Europe](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/thinktank/en/document/LDM_BRI(2012)120306) included the following milestone: a shift from the taxation of labour towards environmental taxation, which would lead to a substantial increase in the share of environmental taxes in government revenue, in line with best practice in EU countries. Figure 7 shows developments in environmental taxes and labour taxes as a result.

[![Image 11: Line chart showing labour taxes and environmental taxes as a share of total taxation in the EU from 2014 to 2024 (index 2014 = 100). Labour taxes remain broadly stable around the 2014 level, whereas environmental taxes decrease markedly after 2021 and remain significantly below their 2014 level in 2022–2024.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/b/bd/SE-ETEA26-Fig04-Taxes_on_labour_and_environmental_taxes_as_share_of_total_taxation.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig04-Taxes_on_labour_and_environmental_taxes_as_share_of_total_taxation.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig04-Taxes_on_labour_and_environmental_taxes_as_share_of_total_taxation.png)

Figure 7: Taxes on labour and environmental taxes as share of total taxation   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en), [(gov_10a_taxag)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10a_taxag/default/table?lang=en)

Between 2014 and 2024, labour tax revenues in the EU remained relatively stable, fluctuating narrowly around the base [index value](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Index_number "Glossary:Index number") of 100, with minor variations between 98.8 and 101.9 until 2020. From 2019 onwards, environmental tax revenues experienced a marked decline, dropping sharply to an index value of 82.8 in 2023 and increasing slightly to an index value of 83.2 in 2024. This represents a 16.8% decrease compared to 2014 levels, highlighting a significant reduction in environmental tax revenues relative to the base year.

## Energy taxes

**Energy taxes: corporations surpass households as primary contributors**

Energy taxes are the primary source of environmental tax revenues in the EU, which is a trend that continued in 2024 for all different payer groups. In the EU, households contributed an average of 43.3% to energy taxes, underlining their key role in final energy consumption (see Figure 8).

[![Image 12: Stacked vertical bar chart showing energy taxes by economic activity as percentage of energy tax revenue in the EU in individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Iceland, and Norway, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/1/10/SE-ETEA26-Fig07-Breakdown_of_Energy.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig07-Breakdown_of_Energy.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig07-Breakdown_of_Energy.png)

Figure 8: Energy taxes by economic activity, 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

**Emission permits**

EU Member States generate substantial revenue through emission permits, which allow holders to release a specific amount of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Under the European [Emissions Trading System (ETS)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Emissions_trading_system_(ETS) "Glossary:Emissions trading system (ETS)"), these permits are classified as taxes according to ESA 2010, the standard used for compiling macroeconomic statistics, including National Accounts. Governments are increasingly using cap-and-trade schemes like the EU ETS to regulate CO2 emissions. Launched in 2005, the EU ETS initially allocated emission allowances for free. Since 2013, however, auctioning has become the primary method for distributing these permits. In the third phase of the ETS (2013–2020), over 70% of allowances were auctioned, and this figure has continued to rise, with phase 4 (2021–2030) introducing a gradual reduction in the total number of emission permits. This phase focuses on protecting sectors at risk of relocating production outside the EU by providing 100% free permits, while free allocations for less exposed sectors will be phased out after 2026. Revenue from ETS auctions is recorded as "other taxes on production" (D.29) under ESA 2010. This means the revenue is recognised in the year the permits are used for emissions, rather than when they are auctioned.

In 2024, EU countries reported €31.3 billion in revenues from EU emissions trading system (ETS) allowances (see Figure 9), representing a 3.5% decrease compared with 2023. Between 2014 and 2024, the marked growth, particularly after 2017, reflects strengthening carbon pricing and the expanding role of emissions trading.

In 2024, Poland (€5.7 billion) and Germany (€5.5 billion) were the largest contributors, while Spain and Italy each reported revenues exceeding €3 billion. Although revenues from ETS allowances declined in Hungary and Luxembourg, most Member States recorded increases. In total the EU aggregate increased by 3.5% in 2024. Overall, the data underline the continued importance of the EU ETS as a key instrument for carbon pricing across the European Union.

[![Image 13: Combined bar and line chart showing total EU tax revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and its annual growth rate from 2014 to 2024. ETS tax revenue increases strongly over the period, while the growth rate peaks in 2019 before slowing and turning slightly negative in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/b/be/SE-ETEA26-Fig08-Total_EU_tax_revenue_from_ETS.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig08-Total_EU_tax_revenue_from_ETS.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig08-Total_EU_tax_revenue_from_ETS.png)

Figure 9: Total EU tax revenue from [ETS](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:ETS "Glossary:ETS"), 2014-2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

## Transport taxes

**Transport taxes: households shoulder the majority of the burden**

This category covers taxes on energy production and on energy products used for both transportation and stationary applications. Key transport fuels include petrol and diesel, while energy sources for stationary use comprise fuel oils, natural gas, coal, and electricity. Taxes on [biofuels](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Biofuels "Glossary:Biofuels") and other [renewable energy sources](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources "Glossary:Renewable energy sources") are also included, as well as taxes on energy product stockpiles. Transport taxes, typically applied to vehicle purchases and road usage, have tended to fluctuate in line with vehicle sales.

In 2024, transport tax revenues in the EU amounted to €67.0 billion, of which €44.6 billion (66.6%) were paid by households, €21.7 billion (32.4%) by industries, and €0.7 billion (1.1%) by non-residents (see Figure 10). Compared with 2023, transport tax revenue increased for all payer groups, with the largest relative increase recorded in taxes paid by non-residents (+13.9%), although these represented only a small share of total transport tax revenue. Households remained the principal contributors to transport tax revenues throughout the EU.

[![Image 14: Stacked vertical bar chart showing transport taxes by economic activity as percentage of transport tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/2/2c/SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png)

Figure 10: Transport taxes by paying economic activities, 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, households were by far the main contributors to transport tax revenues in the EU, accounting for 66.6% on average. This reflects the strong link between transport taxes and private vehicle ownership and use. Transport taxes include, in particular, vehicle registration taxes and other related taxes. The services sector followed with 23.1%, while industry (8.2%), agriculture (1.1%), and non-residents (1.1%) made up smaller shares.

National patterns vary widely: Ireland (80.4%), Malta (78.7%), and Finland (76.2%) show particularly high household shares, indicating a tax structure focused on private vehicle users. In contrast, Slovakia (11.4%) and Czechia (11.5%) report much lower household shares, with the bulk of transport taxes paid by businesses, especially in the services sector, which contributes over 55% in both countries. These differences reflect national transport habits, tax policies, and vehicle ownership trends across Europe.

## Pollution and resource taxes

**Pollution and resource taxes: data indicate a diverse approach across the EU**

For 2024, pollution and resource taxes remain the smallest category with a consistent upward trend (see Figure 11). Starting at about €10 billion in 2008, they increased to around €17.9 billion in 2024. This reflects a growing recognition of the need to address broader environmental issues, not just energy and transportation, but the more extensive impact of resource use and pollution.

[![Image 15: Stacked vertical bar chart showing transport taxes by economic activity as percentage of pollution and resource tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/thumb/a/a8/SE-ETEA26-Fig10-Breakdown_of_Taxes_on_PollutionRes.png/700px-SE-ETEA26-Fig10-Breakdown_of_Taxes_on_PollutionRes.png)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:SE-ETEA26-Fig10-Breakdown_of_Taxes_on_PollutionRes.png)

Figure 11: Pollution and resource taxes by paying economic activities, 2024   
_Source:_ Eurostat [(env_ac_taxind2)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en)

In 2024, pollution and resource tax revenues in the EU were mainly paid by households (44.1%), followed by industries (31.5%), and the services sector (18.8%). The share from agriculture remained relatively small, averaging 2.8%, while non-residents contributed 2.0%. The distribution of these taxes reflects the varying ways countries apply environmental taxes and levies, with some focusing more on household-level waste and pollution charges, and others on industrial emissions or resource use. Overall, the data indicates a diverse approach across the EU to taxing environmental impacts beyond energy and transport.

## Conclusion

Environmental taxes should not be interpreted independently of other environmental accounts—they are embedded within the broader framework of monetary environmental accounts and closely linked to related statistical areas such as Environmental Protection Expenditure Accounts (EPEA), Environmental Subsidies and Similar Transfers (ESST), and potentially environmentally damaging subsidies (PEDS). At the same time, analysing environmental tax revenues alongside other datasets—such as [air emission accounts](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Air_emissions_accounts_(AEA) "Glossary:Air emissions accounts (AEA)") or energy balances—provides valuable insights into the interactions between economic instruments and environmental pressures. This integrated perspective supports more comprehensive and effective policy analysis and decision-making.

## Source data for tables and graphs

*   ![Image 16: Excel](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/0/0b/Excel.jpg)[Environmental tax statistics — figures and tables](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/5/59/SE26-ETEA-v3.xlsx "SE26-ETEA-v3.xlsx")

## Data sources

Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes at a detailed level, by economic activity, under [Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/691/oj/eng) on European environmental economic accounts. The Eurostat publication titled '[Environmental taxes — a statistical guide](http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-GQ-23-016&language=en)' constitutes the methodological basis for this data collection. In addition, using 'National Tax Lists', a supporting dataset to Table 9 from the ESA transmission programme, Eurostat gathers data on environmental taxes for 3 categories: energy, transport, and pollution/resource taxes. The data are then validated and published.

Data relating to environmental taxes can be used to analyse the revenue stream from such taxes and to provide a relative measure of the importance of these taxes through the calculation of ratios relative to GDP or to the total revenue from all taxes and social contributions. In the first case (ratio relative to GDP), the comparison helps to provide an understanding of the tax burden. In the second case, the comparison helps to assess whether or not the tax burden is shifting from other tax bases (for example, labour income) towards environmental taxes. It has to be noted that the total revenue of taxes and social contributions used to compute the ratio does not include imputed social contributions. For further information concerning various tax aggregates, see ['Main national accounts tax aggregates'](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/974dcfe2-4a39-4870-b8a3-70d58f56ff79?lang=en).

Environmental tax revenue can also be allocated according to the different economic activities paying the taxes. Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes using a categorisation by economic activity (based on the [NACE Rev. 2](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE) "Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)") classification supplemented by information for households, non-residents, and a residual category for taxes that could not be allocated).

Increasing revenue from environmental taxes should be interpreted with caution. The increases may be caused by the introduction of new taxes or an increase in tax rates, or alternatively may be linked to an increase in the tax base caused, for instance, by a higher consumption of energy products.

## Context

In today’s economy, production and consumption decisions have a significant impact on the environment. Environmental policies, in particular fiscal policies through taxes, seek to balance economic growth with ecological sustainability. These environmentally related taxes are based on the ‘polluter-pays’ principle, encouraging more sustainable behaviour while generating revenue to address environmental damage. Environmental taxes are an important policy instrument in the EU’s strategic agenda, aimed at strengthening its competitiveness and ensuring the success of the climate neutrality objective.

Economic instruments for pollution control and natural resource management are an important part of environmental policy in the EU Member States. The range of instruments that are available includes, among others, environmental taxes, fees and charges, tradeable permits, deposit-refund systems, and [subsidies](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Subsidies "Glossary:Subsidies").

The [European Green Deal](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640) creates the context for well-designed tax reforms which boost economic growth and resilience to climate shocks and help contribute to a fairer society and to a just transition. Environmental taxes play a direct role by sending the right price signals and providing the right incentives for sustainable behaviour by producers, users, and consumers.

The use of economic tools for the benefit of the environment is also promoted in Goal 17 of the [EU sustainable development goals](http://ec.europa.eu/environment/sustainable-development/SDGs/implementation/index_en.htm).

# Environmental tax revenue continued to increase in 2018

Statistical news from Statistics Sweden 2019-05-16 9.30

Revenue from environmental taxes continued to increase in 2018 and amounted to SEK 101 billion. This increase is due to increased revenue from energy taxes and new environmental taxes on air travel and chemicals. Environmentally motivated subsidies also increased and amounted to SEK 14 billion in 2018.

Environmental tax revenue to the Government amounted to SEK 101 billion, according to preliminary statistics. This is an increase of SEK 2 billion from 2017, which corresponds to an increase of 2 percent. Following several years of decreasing or static environmental tax revenue in the period 2011–2014, revenue has had an upward trend. Environmental tax revenue in 2018 was the largest ever since the beginning of the time series in 1993.

In 2018, revenue increased from both energy tax on fuels and energy tax on electricity, by SEK 1.6 billion each. At the same time, the tax on the thermal effect of nuclear power was phased out, which contributed downward by SEK 2.6 billion. Revenue from the carbon dioxide tax also decreased by SEK 0.5 billion.

The reason for the continued increase in 2018 in total environmental tax revenue is an increase in the tax on certain chemical substances in electronics, as well as the new tax on air travel. The tax on air travel aims to decrease the climate impact from aviation. In 2018, the tax on air travel generated SEK 1.3 billion in revenue. The tax on certain chemicals was introduced on 1 July 2017, which means 2018 is the first year that tax revenue is based on a whole year. Revenue from the tax on certain chemicals amounted to SEK 1.4 billion in 2018.

## Environmental taxes in the EU

The elections to the European Parliament will take place on 26 May in Sweden. However, what taxes apply and the amount of tax paid by EU citizens is decided at national level. The size and significance of environmental taxes varies in different countries.

Statistics on environmental taxes are available in all EU Member States and the taxes are contained in the categories energy taxes, transport taxes, pollution taxes and resource taxes. Comparisons of environmental tax revenue between countries are often made as a share of total tax revenue or GDP, to adjust for the countries’ different sizes. Greece, Slovenia and Denmark were the countries with highest environmental taxes as a share of GDP in 2017. Sweden is among the countries with lower environmental taxes as a share of GDP, at 2.2 percent.

A low or high share can depend on several factors. Environmental tax revenue depends on what environmental taxes apply, tax rates, exceptions in different sectors, as well as the use of the tax base. When the consumption of, for example, fossil fuels decreases, tax revenue also decreases. Even though Sweden often has high tax rates in relation to other countries on, for example, carbon emissions, other factors may also have an impact. Factors can include low tax incomes from transport taxes and a low share of fossil fuels in final consumption.

## Environmentally motivated subsidies

In 2018, environmentally motivated subsidies amounted to SEK 13.8 billion. This is an increase of 40 percent compared with 2017 and the highest level since the beginning of the times series in 2000. The largest contribution comes from the introduction of climate change investments, which are to be used at local and regional level to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Environmentally motivated subsidies include transactions that help reduce climate and environmental impact and improve natural resources management. Subsidies are increasing in several areas. In the agricultural sector, subsidies are increasing following the introduction of “greening” in 2015. International aid has also increased since efforts within the 2030 Agenda began. Actions for renewable energy and energy efficiency continue to increase, including national contributions to the municipalities for the establishment of wind power.

These subsidies, that is, Government contributions for investments and consumption, are allocated to different actors, both nationally and internationally. Subsidies to enterprises, non-profit organisations and other government agencies have increased substantially since 2017 and account for 83 percent of total subsidies. The subsidies have been mostly designated for environmentally related improvements in agriculture and energy, and environmentally related research, for which Swedish enterprises have received support. Subsidies to the rest of the world, in the form of aid and international cooperation on the environment and climate, have increased from SEK 1.7 billion in 2017 to SEK 2.3 billion in 2018.

## Environmentally related subsidies revised

In 2019, a revision of the statistics was conducted. Within the group of international aid, some appropriations were removed for 2008–2017. These appropriations focused on reform cooperation and economic and socially sustainable development. This has led to slower development of international aid in the statistics compared to previously published statistics.

## Definitions and explanations

**Environmental taxes**The definition of an environmental tax that Statistics Sweden applies was developed by Eurostat and the OECD. The term is included in the global SEEA Central Framework statistical standards and enables comparative studies between different countries. The definition is:

“...it has been chosen to single out the tax base that seems to have a particular environmental relevance, and to consider all taxes levied on these tax bases as environmentally related regardless of motives behind their introduction, their names etc.”

Consequently, based on this definition, the tax base determines whether or not a tax is defined as environmental.

Statistics Sweden has presented statistics on environmental taxes since 1993.

**Environmentally motivated subsidies**  
Environmentally motivated subsidies are defined in accordance with the SEEA Central Framework statistical standards for environmental accounts. The definition that applies in Statistics Sweden’s environmental accounts is informed by the subsidy objective. Therefore, the definition used in the environmental accounts is broader than the one used in the national accounts, as the environmental accounts also include capital and current transfers and social benefits in kind.

For the environmental accounts, the primary source for the subsidy objective has been the Government’s Budget Bills for various years. These statistics are derived from the National Financial Management Authority’s calculations of the central government budget’s outcome, in which transactions are traced back to the government appropriations from which they came. In 2015, Statistics Sweden carried out a development project that reviewed the methodology of the statistics.

Statistics Sweden has presented statistics on environmentally motivated subsidies since 2000.

Brussels – Environmental tax revenues rose between 2023 and 2024, but as a proportion of GDP they were lower than ten years earlier, [according to data released by Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260722-1), the EU’s statistical office. Environmental tax revenue in the European Union rose to 371.9 billion euros in 2024 from 350.4 billion euros in 2023. This represents a 6.1 per cent increase (+21.4 billion euros). However, “**despite this increase**, **the share of environmental taxes in the EU’s gross domestic product(GDP) declined from 2.5% in 2014 to 2.1% in 2024.**” Furthermore, over the same period, environmental tax revenue as a percentage of total public revenue from taxes and social security contributions fell from 6.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Significant differences remained between the various countries. Bulgaria (9.7 per cent) and Greece (9.4 per cent) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial declines over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7 per cent), Slovenia (7.3 per cent), Latvia (7.2 per cent), and Poland (7 per cent). At the other end, Luxembourg recorded the lowest rate (2.9 per cent), followed by Sweden (3.9 per cent), and Norway (4 per cent). While most countries showed only modest year-on-year changes, significant increases were observed in Italy, where the proportion rose from 5.5 per cent in 2022 to 6.5 per cent in 2024, and in Hungary, from 5.2 per cent in 2022 to 5.8 per cent in 2024. “Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at the EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe,” Eurostat said. More specifically, energy taxes accounted for over three-quarters (77.2 per cent) of total environmental tax revenue in the EU, reaching 287 billion euros in 2024 from 269.3 billion euros the previous year. Transport taxes (18 per cent of the total) amounted to 67 billion euros in 2024 compared with 64 billion euros in 2023, while taxes on pollution and resources (4.8 per cent) totalled 17.9 billion euros compared with €17.2 billion in 2023. The figures show that environmental tax revenue increased in 22 EU countries in 2024. Romania recorded the highest growth (+21.7 per cent), followed by Lithuania and Poland, with 13.9 per cent and 12.7 per cent, respectively. Hungary (+12.2 per cent) and Poland (+11.2 per cent) are also among the countries with the highest increases. Brussels – Environmental tax revenues rose between 2023 and 2024, but as a proportion of GDP they were lower than ten years earlier, [according to data released by Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260722-1), the EU’s statistical office. Environmental tax revenue in the European Union rose to 371.9 billion euros in 2024 from 350.4 billion euros in 2023. This represents a 6.1 per cent increase (+21.4 billion euros). However, “**despite this increase**, **the share of environmental taxes in the EU’s gross domestic product(GDP) declined from 2.5% in 2014 to 2.1% in 2024.**” Furthermore, over the same period, environmental tax revenue as a percentage of total public revenue from taxes and social security contributions fell from 6.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Significant differences remained between the various countries. Bulgaria (9.7 per cent) and Greece (9.4 per cent) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial declines over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7 per cent), Slovenia (7.3 per cent), Latvia (7.2 per cent), and Poland (7 per cent). At the other end, Luxembourg recorded the lowest rate (2.9 per cent), followed by Sweden (3.9 per cent), and Norway (4 per cent). While most countries showed only modest year-on-year changes, significant increases were observed in Italy, where the proportion rose from 5.5 per cent in 2022 to 6.5 per cent in 2024, and in Hungary, from 5.2 per cent in 2022 to 5.8 per cent in 2024. “Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at the EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe,” Eurostat said. More specifically, energy taxes accounted for over three-quarters (77.2 per cent) of total environmental tax revenue in the EU, reaching 287 billion euros in 2024 from 269.3 billion euros the previous year. Transport taxes (18 per cent of the total) amounted to 67 billion euros in 2024 compared with 64 billion euros in 2023, while taxes on pollution and resources (4.8 per cent) totalled 17.9 billion euros compared with €17.2 billion in 2023. The figures show that environmental tax revenue increased in 22 EU countries in 2024. Romania recorded the highest growth (+21.7 per cent), followed by Lithuania and Poland, with 13.9 per cent and 12.7 per cent, respectively. Hungary (+12.2 per cent) and Poland (+11.2 per cent) are also among the countries with the highest increases. Definition

Environmental taxes are environmentally related tax revenues.

The characteristics of such taxes include revenue, tax base, tax rates and exemptions. They are applied on the following environmental domains: energy products (including vehicle fuels); motor vehicles and transport services; measured or estimated emissions to air and water, ozone depleting substances, certain non-point sources of water pollution, waste management and noise, as well as management of water, land, soil, forests, biodiversity, wildlife and fish stocks.

This indicator is measured as a percentage of GDP and of tax revenue.

Environmental tax revenues in Europe:
structural estimation models

Marius CONSTANTIN

Abstract. Environmental problems mitigation and the transition towards a
greener  economy  with  the  objective  of  becoming  climate  neutral  is  made
possible  through  environmental  regulations.  Environmental  taxes  can  be
considered  one  of  the  best  instruments  needed  when  elaborating  and
implementing environmental protection policies, especially because they act
as vectors of change that can ensure achieving the sustainable development
goals. On the other hand, greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere rose
to new records in 2019 and act as obstacles in becoming climate neutral and
achieving the Goal 13 of sustainable development, the latter addressing the
urgent  need  to  adopt  measures  meant  to  combat  climate  change  and  its
impact,  therefore  measures  designed  to  de-carbonize  economic  activities,
especially  in  countries  with  higher  emissions  of  greenhouse  gases.  In  this
context, the main objective undertook in this research paper was to estimate
the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues  based  on  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in the case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Results highlight strong correlations and statistically significant between the
amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  two  types  of  environmental  tax
revenues:  energy  and  transport.  The  linear  cross–sectional  econometric
methodology (least-squares method) was applied to the data referring to the
year 2018. However, results point to the fact that the only valid econometric
model  constructed  is  the  one  estimating  the  transport  environmental  tax
revenues based on the levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

pp.42 ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020
