# Denmark

## Corporate - Other taxes

Last reviewed - 31 July 2026

## Value-added tax (VAT)

The general VAT rate is 25% of the price charged (exclusive of VAT).

While certain supplies are subject to VAT exemptions, such as hospital treatment, insurance and reinsurance services, and most financial activities, including deposits of money and granting of loans, it is crucial to emphasise a substantial distinction between VAT exempt transactions as per Section 13 and 'zero-rated' transactions under Section 34 in the Danish VAT Act. The aforementioned examples specifically illustrate Section 13 transactions, where the right to reclaim VAT is not applicable. Conversely, transactions falling under Section 34, e.g. intra-community supply of goods and services, allow for a full VAT deduction, highlighting a notable difference in the treatment of these two categories.

Denmark was one of the first countries to introduce a VAT system. Since then, the VAT legislation in Denmark has undergone several changes. The most important changes have been modifications to bring the legislation in line with the Sixth EC VAT Directive (which, since 1 January 2007, is officially named the Council Directive 2006/112/EC on the common system of Value Added Tax) and the so-called EU VAT Package that entered into force on 1 January 2010.

The present Danish VAT Act (_Momsloven_) entered into force with effect from 1 July 1994. Compared to the Directive, the Danish VAT legislation includes minor deviations and the use of various discretionary provisions.

All supplies of goods and services by so-called ‘taxable persons’ (entrepreneurs who independently carry out economic activities) are subject to VAT, unless specifically exempted. Although the VAT exemptions are restricted to a limited range of services and goods, they are subject to a considerable number of binding rulings and administrative guidance with respect to their interpretation and application.

Transactions are subject to Danish VAT only when they are deemed to take place in Denmark. For the sake of tax neutrality, VAT is also levied on (i) imports (i.e. receipt of goods from non-EU territories), (ii) intra-Community acquisitions (i.e. receipt of goods from EU member states), and (iii) purchases of most services from foreign suppliers.

In order to avoid VAT being borne by anyone other than the final consumer, those who qualify as taxable persons can, with some exceptions, recover VAT charged by their suppliers according to the invoice/credit method, provided that the purchases relate to VATable transactions. VAT is recovered either via the periodical VAT return (as a deduction in VAT payable) or by filing a special application.

As a main rule, it is the supplier’s responsibility to settle and report VAT on the supplies of goods and services in Denmark. However, a taxable customer/recipient is responsible for reporting VAT on the import or acquisition of goods from abroad as well as the purchase of most types of services from foreign suppliers. This reverse-charge mechanism also applies to certain specific categories of goods (i.e. electronic devices like smartphones or laptops) traded within Denmark.

### Special payroll tax (Lønsumsafgift)

Companies that provide VAT-exempt services may be liable to pay special payroll tax (in Danish ‘_lønsumsafgift_’) in Denmark, which is calculated on the total payroll, including any type of wages and bonuses that the employee has received. There are four different calculation methods; which method should be applied depends on the activity and organisational structure. The method and percentage applied to calculate the special payroll tax depend on the ratio between VATable and VAT-exempt services supplied.

In case the VAT-exempt financial revenue is more than 50% of the total revenue, the company will be qualified as a financial services provider and the special payroll tax is then 15.3% (for 2021 and the subsequent years) of the payroll used for the VAT-exempt activities.

This tax is deductible for income tax purposes.

## Customs duties

Denmark is a member state of the European Union, and, according to EU’s Common Customs Tariff, goods imported into Denmark from outside the European Union are subject to customs duties. The rates of duty vary widely between goods. Once goods have been customs cleared in any EU member state, they may circulate freely within the European Union.

## Excise duties

According to Danish tax law, several excise duties are levied on different products. Some of the excise duties are enacted based on EU regulations while others are enacted according to domestic law only.

Excise duties are chargeable on a long list of goods, including (but not only) oil products, certain packaging, alcoholic drinks and tobacco, chocolate and sweets, coffee, etc.

The excise duty rates depend on the type of goods (e.g. chocolate, packaging) as well as, in some cases, the category of the goods (e.g. plastic bags, paper bags). Furthermore, many of the excise duty rates are regulated every year.

Only goods sold in Denmark (or taken into Denmark) are liable to the Danish excise duties. Companies taking goods into Denmark or companies producing goods in Denmark must be registered with the Danish tax authorities to settle the excise duties.

The type of registration is decisive for when the companies must pay the excise duties.

As excise duties are a tax for consumption in Denmark, a company can, in principle, obtain a reimbursement of the excise duties on products sold outside of Denmark. Companies are entitled to a reimbursement even if the company is not registered for the excise duties in question and even if the excise duties have been paid by previous resellers, etc.

## Property taxes

The Danish property tax system has recently been revised, so all property taxes for 2022 and onwards are preliminary, and any adjustment will be claimed backwards once the assessments are final.The finalisation of the property taxes is pending the publication of the final assessments, which is currently expected to be in 2025/26.

Owners of non-residential property must pay land tax annually. The land tax rate is set by the municipalities and is between 0.31% and 1.77% of the value of the land. Municipalities may also levy a special coverage charge on certain non-residential properties at a rate also set by the municipalities and is between 0.08% and 1.8% of the land value.

It is important to note that there are several transitional schemes in the new legislation, to ensure that neither private nor commercial individuals will receive greatly increased claims in the new system. However, making changes to the property could void these schemes and have a great impact on the property taxes.

## Stamp tax

Stamp tax is payable on a few documents, including deeds for the transfer of real estate, and mortgages associated with real estate and cooperative housing, chattels, and intangible assets, as well as property reservations in motor vehicles. There is no stamp duty on the transfer of shares.

The stamp tax is a fixed amount of DKK 1,850 (2026), accompanied by a predetermined percentage of 1.25% (2026) based on the fixed fee (DKK 1,850 and 1.25%) for security in immovable property.

## Payroll taxes

There are no payroll taxes other than employer’s tax (_see below_).

## Employer’s tax (social security charges)

The employer’s contribution to _Arbejdsmarkedets Tillægspension_ (ATP) (i.e. old-age pension) charges is DKK 2,376 (2026) _per annum_ for a full-time employee and DKK 1,188 (2026) for the employee part.

Based on the ATP contribution, derived contributions will be due. Also, a mandatory Danish accidents at work insurance must be taken out. The total annual employer social security costs are approximately DKK 16,000 (2026) per full time employee depending on industry.

Employers that pay ATP contributions are also liable of making contributions to the Danish Labour Market Fund for Posted Workers, although this is not a social security contribution.

Companies that provide VAT-exempt services are liable to pay the employer’s tax, which is calculated on the total annual salary cost. The rate can be as high as 15.3%, which is the rate from 2018 and onwards for banks and other financial institutions, the most significant sector paying the employer’s tax. This tax is deductible for income tax purposes.

## Environmental taxes / Energy taxes

Danish companies must pay environmental taxes, which were introduced to reduce companies’ energy consumption, discharges of fluids with an environmental impact, and emission. These taxes are paid to the companies that provide the energy, who then pay the taxes to the Danish tax authorities. Most of the environmental tax rates are regulated every year.

In general, in 2025 almost all VAT-registered companies in Denmark could obtain a reimbursement of some of the environmental taxes on energy (also called energy taxes). The size of the reimbursement of the energy taxes depends on the type of energy used and to what extent the companies can deduct VAT.

From 1 January 2025, a new CO2 tax entered into effect. This tax represents a significant change to the Danish excise duty system and has notably affected the reimbursement of excise duties on energy.

Abstract. Environmental problems mitigation and the transition towards a
greener  economy  with  the  objective  of  becoming  climate  neutral  is  made
possible  through  environmental  regulations.  Environmental  taxes  can  be
considered  one  of  the  best  instruments  needed  when  elaborating  and
implementing environmental protection policies, especially because they act
as vectors of change that can ensure achieving the sustainable development
goals. On the other hand, greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere rose
to new records in 2019 and act as obstacles in becoming climate neutral and
achieving the Goal 13 of sustainable development, the latter addressing the
urgent  need  to  adopt  measures  meant  to  combat  climate  change  and  its
impact,  therefore  measures  designed  to  de-carbonize  economic  activities,
especially  in  countries  with  higher  emissions  of  greenhouse  gases.  In  this
context, the main objective undertook in this research paper was to estimate
the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues  based  on  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in the case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Results highlight strong correlations and statistically significant between the
amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  two  types  of  environmental  tax
revenues:  energy  and  transport.  The  linear  cross–sectional  econometric
methodology (least-squares method) was applied to the data referring to the
year 2018. However, results point to the fact that the only valid econometric
model  constructed  is  the  one  estimating  the  transport  environmental  tax
revenues based on the levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

Introduction
In  a  global  context  marked  by  the  green  development
movement,  environmental  tax  revenues  represent  one  of  the  main
sources  to  generate  public  revenue  in  the  spirit  of  bringing
environmental  issues  to  the  attention  of  citizens.  In  contemporary
economies,  environmental  taxation  represents  a  key  tool  for
promoting  environmentally  friendly  technologies,  but,  above  all,
environmental taxation shapes responsible behaviors and consolidates
specific  dedicated  policies  (Dinu  et  al.,  2020),  especially  taking  into
account the negative effects of phenomena such as biodiversity loss,
degradation of ecosystems and the more sensitive air pollution. In this
context, environmental tax revenues represents a relevant indicator for
understanding specific environmental policies. Not only that, but also
environmental  tax  revenues  aim  at  mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful
actions  against  the  environment  in  a  resource-efficient  manner.
Economic instruments for pollution control and efficient management
of  natural  resources  represent  an  essential  part  in  the  case  of  the
environmental and energy policies in the European Union.
Environmental  tax  revenues  can  be  used  to  address
environmental  issues,  such  as:  poor  waste  disposal,  high  levels  of
pollution  of  any  kind:  water,  air,  soil,  and  other  forms  of
environmental  issues.  In  this  context,  as  is  argues  in  numerous
literature  (Villar‐Rubio  &  Huete‐Morales,  2017;  Andreoni,  2019;
Torney, 2019; Cadoret et al., 2020), no matter the nature of policies
which  imply  designing  and  implementing  measures  specific  to
resorting to environmental tax revenues – all these policies are highly
depended  on  their  socio-economic  substantiation.  Moreover,  one  of
the  instruments  used  to  influence  the  economic  behaviors  of
consumers  and  producers  towards  sustainability  has  been  the
environmental  tax  revenues  –  a  flexible  cost-effective  manner  for
harnessing the polluter-pays principle among the European citizens.
As it is shown in (European Commission, 2019a), during 2018,
the  governments  of  countries  part  of  the  European  Union  collected
324.6  billion  €  of  environmental  tax  revenues,  representing  2.4%  of

DOI: 10.2478/9788366675261-004
pp. 43  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 3]
the European Union’s GDP and 6.0% of the total government revenue
coming from social contributions and taxes.
As referring to its distribution, according to the calculus based
on Eurostat, (2020) and European Commission, (2019a), nevertheless,
approximately  78%  of  the  total  environmental  tax  revenues  comes
from the energy sector, approximately 19% represents transport taxes,
and  the  rest  (approximately  3%)  comes  from  taxes  on  pollution and
resources,  therefore  the  latter  having  a  small  share  out  of  the  total
taxes.
According  to  (European  Commission,  2019),  the  European
Green  Deal  is  ensuring  that  taxation  is  aligned  with  the  objectives
specific  to  climate  change  is essential  and  delivering  the  European
Green Deal can be made possible only by rethinking national budgets
as the means of the transition for a cleaner European economy – and
not  only.  Better  management  of  green  budgeting  instruments  will
contribute  to  redirecting  consumption  behaviors,  production  patterns
and taxation to green priorities in the European Union. The transition
to  the  green  circular  economy  –  sustainable  in  terms  of  resource
allocation, availability and use, it calls for the implementation of more
efficient  and  environmentally  responsible  taxation  frameworks.  This
green  transition  requires  both  the  modernization  of  environmental
taxation systems and the expansion of opportunities for promoting and
implementing clean, environmentally friendly technologies  – capable
of generating higher levels of added-value, therefore technologies that
are economically competitive on global markets.
Environmental policies also involve frameworks and actions in
relation  to  climate  change  strategies  and  such  policies  have  a
significant fiscal component. The latter is  based on a comprehensive
sanction  mechanism  –  compensation  specific  to  environmental
taxation. From this perspective, a relevant example is that through the
new  Circular  Economy  Action  Plan  for  a  cleaner  and  more
competitive Europe (European Commission, 2020), among others, the
European  Union  aims  at  ―achieving  climate  neutrality  by  2050  and
decoupling economic growth from resource use‖. In order to ensure a
climate-neutral, circular and resource-efficient economy, the European
Commission will propose policies that can also include references to
environmental taxes – as means of achieving climate neutrality.

[PDF page 4]
According  to  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambitions  (European
Commission, 2020), the greenhouse  gas emissions are to be reduced
of at least 55% by 2030 compared to the year 1990, as it is considered
to improve the wellbeing of EU citizens and to support the COVID-19
recovery,  along  with  the  resilience  and  competitiveness  of  the
European  economy.  In  this  context,  the  EU  taxonomy  will  be  an
essential  instrument  to  bring  finance  closer  to  the  needs  of  the
transition to a cleaner economy. Since it is argued that high levels of
environmental tax revenues can contribute to raising the quality of the
environment  and  environmental  protection  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-
Chudzio,  2017) and  taking  into  consideration  the  importance  for  the
EU  members  to  facilitate  the  transition  to  a  circular  and  climate-
neutral  economy  through  EU  taxonomy,  the  main  objective  of  this
research  was  to  design  a  cross–sectional  linear  regression  model
meant  to  estimate  the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues
structurally based on the  amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the
case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the
year 2018 as the reference point for this study.

Literature review
In  the  European  Union,  the  evolution  of  environmental  tax
revenues is grounded in the historical heritage of each country and it is
influenced by socio-economic aspects such as the degree of economic
development,  size  of  the  population,  consumption  and  production
behaviors and other factors (Štreimikienė, 2015).
Through  environmental  tax  revenues,  the  European  Union
member  states  provide  disincentives  to  consumption  and  build
towards  a  more  green,  environmentally-friendly  economic
development  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-Chudzio,  2019). European  states
which  have  implemented  reforms  concerning  the  topic  of
environmental  tax  revenues  have  achieved  their  socio-economic  and
environmental  objectives  more  efficiently  than  those  who  did  not
focus,  for  various  reasons,  on  elaborating  and  implementing  well-
thought  environmental  tax  collecting  reforms  (Miceikiene  et  al.,
2016).
However, this is not only the case of the European Union. Fan,
Li  and  Yin  (2019)  mathematically  confirmed  that  imposing

DOI: 10.2478/9788366675261-004
pp. 45  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 5]
environmental  tax  significantly  contributes  to  achieving  green
development, based on a small set of data referring to China. On the
other  hand,  Still,  Piciu,  Ipate  and  Bogdan  (2016)  argue  that
environmental  taxes  should  not  only  act  as  a  tool  for  building  a
cleaner economy, but rather it must also contribute to obtaining a fair
market  price,  in  consonance  with  both  the  results  coming  from  the
economic scientific research teams and from the political will.
Tantau, Maassen and Fratila (2018) designed a panel regression model
meant  to  determine  the  dependency  between  indicators  that  assess
progress  of  the  circular  economy  in  Europe.  In  the  constructed
econometric model, the authors included environmental tax revenues
as  one  of  the  main  independent  variables,  which  proved  to  be
significant  within  the  regression  model  in  relation  to  the  rest  of  the
independent variables and in relation to the dependent variable – the
recycling rate of municipal waste, at the level of the EU-28 members,
corresponding to the 2010-2014 period.
An econometric study carried out at the level of the European
Union level concerning the 2010-2017 period highlights how strategic
and  careful  socio-economic  and  ecological  policies  must  be
constructed,  since  an  increase  of  the  expenses  concerning
environmental  taxes  could  eventually  act  as  an  impediment  for
potential investors in future ecological projects (Banacu et al., 2019),
even  though  taxes  would  initially  be  designed  to  harness  the
implementation of green initiatives.
Through a panel smooth transition regression approach, Cepoi,
Bran  and  Dinu  (2020)  suggest  that  European  countries  should
implement measures designed to avoid environmental degradation by
intensifying the use of biofuels and not only relying on environmental
taxes.
Chu,  Cheng  and  Lai  (2018)  proved  the  importance  of  the
distribution  of  environmental  tax  revenues  per  generations.  They
demonstrated  that  this  form  of  tax  revenues  must  be  considered
according  to  the  needs  and  possibilities  of  both  the  young  and  old
generations. The authors argue that raising environmental taxes could
potentially  generate  inter-generational  conflicts  concerning  the
environmental policy and that would be undesirable considering that
there are ways to appropriately establish thresholds for environmental

DOI: 10.2478/9788366675261-004
pp. 46  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 6]
taxes in such a manner that can assure the long-term improvement of
welfare of all generations.
Merko,  Dursun  and  Merko  (2018)  demonstrated  that  the
environmental tax revenues represent an important share of Albania’s
GDP  (2.77%  on  average)  and  that  this  form  of  revenues  is
characterized  by  an  average  increase  of  4.7%  in  the  same  analyzed
period, 2008-2015. The greatest share of environmental tax revenues
was registered in the case of the energy sector (56.64%).
In other study, Miceikiene  and Ciuleviciene (2016)  identified
some of the factors that influence the environmental tax revenues and
some  of  those  are  the  following:  nominal  GDP,  energy  saving,
municipality-generated  waste, renewable energy production, nominal
environmental protection expenditure and others. Moreover, the same
authors argue that the nominal GDP has the most impactful influence
on the variation of the environmental tax revenues in Lithuania.
However,  other  authors  (Leibus  and  Mazure,  2016)
demonstrated  that  environmental  tax  revenues  have  relatively  small
shares  in  the  case  of  the  Baltic  States.  Considering  the  1994-2012
timeframe  and  the  European  countries  included  in  the  OECD
database,  a  study  (Onofrei  et  al.,  2017)  based  on  panel  data  fixed-
effect estimation techniques empirically proved that environmental tax
revenues  represent  an  important  vector  designed  to  reduce  pollution
levels,  especially  when  approached  in  relation  to  the  generation  of
greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Speck  (2017)  argues  that  decreasing
greenhouse  gas  emissions  in  the  European  Union  by  80-95%  by  the
year 2050 reported to the 1990 year levels will determine a decrease
of the tax base of both the energy taxes and carbon pricing.

environmental  tax  revenues,  split  per  component  (energy,  transport
and pollution & resources) – as included in Table 1.

Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
The  greenhouse  gas  emissions  indicator  is  part  of  the  EU
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDG)  designed  to  assess  progress
towards  Goal  13  on  climate  action.  Part  of  the  2030  Agenda  for
Sustainable  Development  (United  Nations,  2015),  SDG  13  aims  to
implement  the  commitment  to  climate  change objectives  and  reduce
the  amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Such  measures  are
furthermore  encouraged  by  the  European  Green  Deal,  Circular
Economy  Action  Plan  and  part  of  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambition.
The indicator quantifies total national emissions, international aviation
included. Gases include carbon  dioxide,  methane,  nitrous  oxide,  and
F-gases. Using the individual global warming potential of each of the
gases, they are expressed in units of carbon dioxide equivalents.
As described by Eurostat (2020), environmental  tax revenues
are  part  of  the  environmental  accounts  that  constitute  a  satellite
account  to  national  accounts.  This  indicator  is  split  per  category,  as
described in Table 1. Eurostat considers an environmental tax any tax
whose  base  is  a  physical  unit  of  actions  that  has  a  proven  negative
impact on the natural capital. In order for payments to be identified as
environmental taxes, they must be tracked in the national accounts as
environmental taxes. Other forms of payments to government are not
considered  revenues based on environmental taxes. It is important to

The  research  method  used  in  this  study  is  econometric.
Multiple  cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  designed  in
order  to  find  the  best  model  for  estimating  the  amount  of
environmental tax revenues (i.e.: best tax revenue category), based on
the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  generated  by  the  selected  European
countries included in this study. In all of the constructed econometric
models,  the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  represent  the  independent
variable  and  the  environmental  tax  revenues  (split  per  category)
represent the dependent variable. This research method is quantitative,
based  on  cross–sectional  statistic  data,  characterized  by  multiple
observations studied at a single moment in time (the year 2018 in this
particular  research),  referring  to  multiple  entities  (i.e.:  European
countries).

Conclusion
The  transition  towards  a  greener  circular  economy  with  the
goal  of becoming  climate neutral is made possible, among other, by
resorting  to  an  important  instrument:  environmental  regulations and,
more  specifically,  environmental  tax  revenues.  The  latter  aim  at
mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful  actions  against  the  environment  in
resources-efficient manners, especially in the European Union.
In  the  case  of  the  analyzed  European  countries,  the  energy
sector  represents  the  major  source  of  environmental  pollution  and,
consequently,  a  corresponding  high  level  of  environmental  tax
revenues.  In  2018,  the  governments  of  the  members  part  of  the
European  Union  collected  324.6  billions  €  of  environmental  tax
revenues, representing 2.4% of the European Union’s GDP.
The environment tax proves to be a real policy instrument for
green development. The European Green Deal ensures that taxation is
aligned  with  the  objectives  specific  to  climate  change.  The  2030
Agenda for Sustainable  Development aims at decreasing the  amount
of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  this  can  be  made  possible  through
environmental taxes, grounded on the polluter-pays principle.
The main objective of this research was achieved, as multiple
cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  constructed  with  the
aim to estimate the amount of environmental tax revenues structurally
based on the amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the case of EU
members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the year 2018
as  the  reference  point  for  this  study. Results  highlight  that  the  only
valid econometric model is that in the case of transport environmental
tax revenues estimated in relation with the generated greenhouse gas
emissions.  The  model  proves  that  one  additional  million  tonne  of

14.5451 million EUR of transport environmental taxes, at the level of
the year 2018, in the case of the analyzed European countries.
The  main  limitation  of  this  study  refers  to  the  fact  that  the
analysis does not encompass historic data of the studied phenomena.
However, this study can be extended by approaching the same subject
in  a  different  manner  –  considering  a  panel  data  approach  and  even
more extend the econometric model with more relevant variables.

Abstract. Environmental problems mitigation and the transition towards a
greener  economy  with  the  objective  of  becoming  climate  neutral  is  made
possible  through  environmental  regulations.  Environmental  taxes  can  be
considered  one  of  the  best  instruments  needed  when  elaborating  and
implementing environmental protection policies, especially because they act
as vectors of change that can ensure achieving the sustainable development
goals. On the other hand, greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere rose
to new records in 2019 and act as obstacles in becoming climate neutral and
achieving the Goal 13 of sustainable development, the latter addressing the
urgent  need  to  adopt  measures  meant  to  combat  climate  change  and  its
impact,  therefore  measures  designed  to  de-carbonize  economic  activities,
especially  in  countries  with  higher  emissions  of  greenhouse  gases.  In  this
context, the main objective undertook in this research paper was to estimate
the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues  based  on  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in the case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Results highlight strong correlations and statistically significant between the
amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  two  types  of  environmental  tax
revenues:  energy  and  transport.  The  linear  cross–sectional  econometric
methodology (least-squares method) was applied to the data referring to the
year 2018. However, results point to the fact that the only valid econometric
model  constructed  is  the  one  estimating  the  transport  environmental  tax
revenues based on the levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

Introduction
In  a  global  context  marked  by  the  green  development
movement,  environmental  tax  revenues  represent  one  of  the  main
sources  to  generate  public  revenue  in  the  spirit  of  bringing
environmental  issues  to  the  attention  of  citizens.  In  contemporary
economies,  environmental  taxation  represents  a  key  tool  for
promoting  environmentally  friendly  technologies,  but,  above  all,
environmental taxation shapes responsible behaviors and consolidates
specific  dedicated  policies  (Dinu  et  al.,  2020),  especially  taking  into
account the negative effects of phenomena such as biodiversity loss,
degradation of ecosystems and the more sensitive air pollution. In this
context, environmental tax revenues represents a relevant indicator for
understanding specific environmental policies. Not only that, but also
environmental  tax  revenues  aim  at  mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful
actions  against  the  environment  in  a  resource-efficient  manner.
Economic instruments for pollution control and efficient management
of  natural  resources  represent  an  essential  part  in  the  case  of  the
environmental and energy policies in the European Union.
Environmental  tax  revenues  can  be  used  to  address
environmental  issues,  such  as:  poor  waste  disposal,  high  levels  of
pollution  of  any  kind:  water,  air,  soil,  and  other  forms  of
environmental  issues.  In  this  context,  as  is  argues  in  numerous
literature  (Villar‐Rubio  &  Huete‐Morales,  2017;  Andreoni,  2019;
Torney, 2019; Cadoret et al., 2020), no matter the nature of policies
which  imply  designing  and  implementing  measures  specific  to
resorting to environmental tax revenues – all these policies are highly
depended  on  their  socio-economic  substantiation.  Moreover,  one  of
the  instruments  used  to  influence  the  economic  behaviors  of
consumers  and  producers  towards  sustainability  has  been  the
environmental  tax  revenues  –  a  flexible  cost-effective  manner  for
harnessing the polluter-pays principle among the European citizens.
As it is shown in (European Commission, 2019a), during 2018,
the  governments  of  countries  part  of  the  European  Union  collected
324.6  billion  €  of  environmental  tax  revenues,  representing  2.4%  of

the European Union’s GDP and 6.0% of the total government revenue
coming from social contributions and taxes.
As referring to its distribution, according to the calculus based

approximately  78%  of  the  total  environmental  tax  revenues  comes
from the energy sector, approximately 19% represents transport taxes,
and  the  rest  (approximately  3%)  comes  from  taxes  on  pollution and
resources,  therefore  the  latter  having  a  small  share  out  of  the  total
taxes.
According  to  (European  Commission,  2019),  the  European
Green  Deal  is  ensuring  that  taxation  is  aligned  with  the  objectives
specific  to  climate  change  is essential  and  delivering  the  European
Green Deal can be made possible only by rethinking national budgets
as the means of the transition for a cleaner European economy – and
not  only.  Better  management  of  green  budgeting  instruments  will
contribute  to  redirecting  consumption  behaviors,  production  patterns
and taxation to green priorities in the European Union. The transition
to  the  green  circular  economy  –  sustainable  in  terms  of  resource
allocation, availability and use, it calls for the implementation of more
efficient  and  environmentally  responsible  taxation  frameworks.  This
green  transition  requires  both  the  modernization  of  environmental
taxation systems and the expansion of opportunities for promoting and
implementing clean, environmentally friendly technologies  – capable
of generating higher levels of added-value, therefore technologies that
are economically competitive on global markets.
Environmental policies also involve frameworks and actions in
relation  to  climate  change  strategies  and  such  policies  have  a
significant fiscal component. The latter is  based on a comprehensive
sanction  mechanism  –  compensation  specific  to  environmental
taxation. From this perspective, a relevant example is that through the
new  Circular  Economy  Action  Plan  for  a  cleaner  and  more
competitive Europe (European Commission, 2020), among others, the
European  Union  aims  at  ―achieving  climate  neutrality  by  2050  and
decoupling economic growth from resource use‖. In order to ensure a
climate-neutral, circular and resource-efficient economy, the European
Commission will propose policies that can also include references to
environmental taxes – as means of achieving climate neutrality.

According  to  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambitions  (European
Commission, 2020), the greenhouse  gas emissions are to be reduced
of at least 55% by 2030 compared to the year 1990, as it is considered
to improve the wellbeing of EU citizens and to support the COVID-19
recovery,  along  with  the  resilience  and  competitiveness  of  the
European  economy.  In  this  context,  the  EU  taxonomy  will  be  an
essential  instrument  to  bring  finance  closer  to  the  needs  of  the
transition to a cleaner economy. Since it is argued that high levels of
environmental tax revenues can contribute to raising the quality of the
environment  and  environmental  protection  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-
Chudzio,  2017) and  taking  into  consideration  the  importance  for  the
EU  members  to  facilitate  the  transition  to  a  circular  and  climate-
neutral  economy  through  EU  taxonomy,  the  main  objective  of  this
research  was  to  design  a  cross–sectional  linear  regression  model
meant  to  estimate  the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues
structurally based on the  amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the
case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the
year 2018 as the reference point for this study.

Literature review
In  the  European  Union,  the  evolution  of  environmental  tax
revenues is grounded in the historical heritage of each country and it is
influenced by socio-economic aspects such as the degree of economic
development,  size  of  the  population,  consumption  and  production
behaviors and other factors (Štreimikienė, 2015).
Through  environmental  tax  revenues,  the  European  Union
member  states  provide  disincentives  to  consumption  and  build
towards  a  more  green,  environmentally-friendly  economic
development  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-Chudzio,  2019). European  states
which  have  implemented  reforms  concerning  the  topic  of
environmental  tax  revenues  have  achieved  their  socio-economic  and
environmental  objectives  more  efficiently  than  those  who  did  not
focus,  for  various  reasons,  on  elaborating  and  implementing  well-
thought  environmental  tax  collecting  reforms  (Miceikiene  et  al.,
2016).
However, this is not only the case of the European Union. Fan,
Li  and  Yin  (2019)  mathematically  confirmed  that  imposing

development, based on a small set of data referring to China. On the
other  hand,  Still,  Piciu,  Ipate  and  Bogdan  (2016)  argue  that
environmental  taxes  should  not  only  act  as  a  tool  for  building  a
cleaner economy, but rather it must also contribute to obtaining a fair
market  price,  in  consonance  with  both  the  results  coming  from  the
economic scientific research teams and from the political will.
Tantau, Maassen and Fratila (2018) designed a panel regression model
meant  to  determine  the  dependency  between  indicators  that  assess
progress  of  the  circular  economy  in  Europe.  In  the  constructed
econometric model, the authors included environmental tax revenues
as  one  of  the  main  independent  variables,  which  proved  to  be
significant  within  the  regression  model  in  relation  to  the  rest  of  the
independent variables and in relation to the dependent variable – the
recycling rate of municipal waste, at the level of the EU-28 members,
corresponding to the 2010-2014 period.
An econometric study carried out at the level of the European
Union level concerning the 2010-2017 period highlights how strategic
and  careful  socio-economic  and  ecological  policies  must  be
constructed,  since  an  increase  of  the  expenses  concerning
environmental  taxes  could  eventually  act  as  an  impediment  for
potential investors in future ecological projects (Banacu et al., 2019),
even  though  taxes  would  initially  be  designed  to  harness  the
implementation of green initiatives.
Through a panel smooth transition regression approach, Cepoi,
Bran  and  Dinu  (2020)  suggest  that  European  countries  should
implement measures designed to avoid environmental degradation by
intensifying the use of biofuels and not only relying on environmental
taxes.
Chu,  Cheng  and  Lai  (2018)  proved  the  importance  of  the
distribution  of  environmental  tax  revenues  per  generations.  They
demonstrated  that  this  form  of  tax  revenues  must  be  considered
according  to  the  needs  and  possibilities  of  both  the  young  and  old
generations. The authors argue that raising environmental taxes could
potentially  generate  inter-generational  conflicts  concerning  the
environmental policy and that would be undesirable considering that
there are ways to appropriately establish thresholds for environmental

environmental  tax  revenues,  split  per  component  (energy,  transport
and pollution & resources) – as included in Table 1.

The  greenhouse  gas  emissions  indicator  is  part  of  the  EU
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDG)  designed  to  assess  progress
towards  Goal  13  on  climate  action.  Part  of  the  2030  Agenda  for
Sustainable  Development  (United  Nations,  2015),  SDG  13  aims  to
implement  the  commitment  to  climate  change objectives  and  reduce
the  amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Such  measures  are
furthermore  encouraged  by  the  European  Green  Deal,  Circular
Economy  Action  Plan  and  part  of  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambition.
The indicator quantifies total national emissions, international aviation
included. Gases include carbon  dioxide,  methane,  nitrous  oxide,  and
F-gases. Using the individual global warming potential of each of the
gases, they are expressed in units of carbon dioxide equivalents.
As described by Eurostat (2020), environmental  tax revenues
are  part  of  the  environmental  accounts  that  constitute  a  satellite
account  to  national  accounts.  This  indicator  is  split  per  category,  as
described in Table 1. Eurostat considers an environmental tax any tax
whose  base  is  a  physical  unit  of  actions  that  has  a  proven  negative
impact on the natural capital. In order for payments to be identified as
environmental taxes, they must be tracked in the national accounts as
environmental taxes. Other forms of payments to government are not
considered  revenues based on environmental taxes. It is important to

The  research  method  used  in  this  study  is  econometric.
Multiple  cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  designed  in
order  to  find  the  best  model  for  estimating  the  amount  of
environmental tax revenues (i.e.: best tax revenue category), based on
the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  generated  by  the  selected  European
countries included in this study. In all of the constructed econometric
models,  the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  represent  the  independent
variable  and  the  environmental  tax  revenues  (split  per  category)
represent the dependent variable. This research method is quantitative,
based  on  cross–sectional  statistic  data,  characterized  by  multiple
observations studied at a single moment in time (the year 2018 in this
particular  research),  referring  to  multiple  entities  (i.e.:  European
countries).

Conclusion
The  transition  towards  a  greener  circular  economy  with  the
goal  of becoming  climate neutral is made possible, among other, by
resorting  to  an  important  instrument:  environmental  regulations and,
more  specifically,  environmental  tax  revenues.  The  latter  aim  at
mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful  actions  against  the  environment  in
resources-efficient manners, especially in the European Union.
In  the  case  of  the  analyzed  European  countries,  the  energy
sector  represents  the  major  source  of  environmental  pollution  and,
consequently,  a  corresponding  high  level  of  environmental  tax
revenues.  In  2018,  the  governments  of  the  members  part  of  the
European  Union  collected  324.6  billions  €  of  environmental  tax
revenues, representing 2.4% of the European Union’s GDP.
The environment tax proves to be a real policy instrument for
green development. The European Green Deal ensures that taxation is
aligned  with  the  objectives  specific  to  climate  change.  The  2030
Agenda for Sustainable  Development aims at decreasing the  amount
of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  this  can  be  made  possible  through
environmental taxes, grounded on the polluter-pays principle.
The main objective of this research was achieved, as multiple
cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  constructed  with  the
aim to estimate the amount of environmental tax revenues structurally
based on the amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the case of EU
members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the year 2018
as  the  reference  point  for  this  study. Results  highlight  that  the  only
valid econometric model is that in the case of transport environmental
tax revenues estimated in relation with the generated greenhouse gas
emissions.  The  model  proves  that  one  additional  million  tonne  of

14.5451 million EUR of transport environmental taxes, at the level of
the year 2018, in the case of the analyzed European countries.
The  main  limitation  of  this  study  refers  to  the  fact  that  the
analysis does not encompass historic data of the studied phenomena.
However, this study can be extended by approaching the same subject
in  a  different  manner  –  considering  a  panel  data  approach  and  even
more extend the econometric model with more relevant variables.

**Taxation in Denmark** consists of a comprehensive system of direct and indirect taxes. Ever since the income tax was introduced in [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") via a fundamental tax reform in 1903, it has been a fundamental pillar in the Danish tax system. Today various personal and corporate income taxes yield around two thirds of the total Danish tax revenues, indirect taxes being responsible for the last third. The state personal income tax is a [progressive tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_tax "Progressive tax") while the municipal income tax is a [proportional tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_tax "Proportional tax") above a certain income level.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Overview")]

The types and levels of taxation in Denmark have changed dramatically since the state's inception. In the sixteenth century, Denmark primarily obtained state income through taxes excised on feudal [Demesne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demesne "Demesne") lands [[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:1-1) and the [Sound Dues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Dues "Sound Dues"), which required foreign ships to pay a toll when passing through the [Øresund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund "Øresund") bordering Denmark. In fact, the Dues comprised two-thirds of Denmark's tax revenue throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-2) The costs of warfare, such as those of the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War"), were further fulfilled by Denmark's heavily [agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture") economy. In later conflicts such as the [Scanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanian_War "Scanian War") and the [Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War "Great Northern War"), however, Denmark ceded much of its territory, resulting in monetary losses that prompted higher tax rates and the introduction of an initially small income tax. Massive population growth resulted in expansion of agriculture and consequently an expansion of taxes gained from tariffs on exports and wheat sales. By 1897, Denmark's income tax encompassed 15.00% [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) of the state's total revenue, far surpassing any other European country at the time. From 1897 to the present, Denmark continued to boast exceptionally high income tax rates, never dropping below the top five countries in Europe in terms of percentage revenue earned from income taxes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) Following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), as with many other countries, Denmark began to enact several social welfare programs, including aid for the sick and the unemployed.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:1-1) These, along with expansion of the [public sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_sector "Public sector") (schools, teachers, etc.) contributed to the income tax being a staple of Denmark's tax revenue.

### Changes in the 20th and 21st Centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Changes in the 20th and 21st Centuries")]

The exact form of income tax has varied through the past century. Between 1903 and 1966, income tax was levied only on "assessed" income, which did not include personal taxes that were spent on other areas, such as to the church. After 1966, income tax was changed to be levied on [taxable income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxable_income "Taxable income"), which included personal taxes spent on other areas and later also included income received from [stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Share_capital "Share capital") and [interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest "Interest").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-4) In recent years, public sentiment[_[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_] towards taxes has leaned towards limiting the [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state") and consequently the income tax. In 2001, a "tax freeze" that prevented the further increase of taxes was administered by the then liberal-conservative government of Denmark. The tax freeze could only be waived in particular times of crisis, and a tax could only be increased at the expense of a different form of tax.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-5) Furthermore, the Danish Tax Reform of 2010 gradually cut taxes "to increase labour supply in the medium to long term and at same time contribute to soften the effects of the global economic crises in the short run."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-6) The tax cuts impacted the high, middle, and low classes, and resulted in a net cut of 30 billion [DKK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_krone "Danish krone") between 2010 and 2019. Despite these policies, income taxes have stabilized at providing around 50% of Denmark's total revenue since 1990.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) According to the [World Happiness Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Happiness_Report "World Happiness Report"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-7) Denmark ranks among the top two in terms of happiness, indicating a general contentedness with the state's welfare state and the benefits provided. The World Happiness Report also states that happiness is correlated to social equality. The official Denmark website remarks that "most Danes will tell you that they are happy to pay taxes because they can see what they get in return," including free tuition, healthcare, and social security.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-8)

### Municipal & National income tax

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Municipal & National income tax")]

All income from employment or self-employment is taxed at 8% before income tax. This tax is termed a "labour market contribution" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _arbejdsmarkedsbidrag_) or colloquially a "gross tax" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _bruttoskat_). The funds levied through this tax support the functions related to the labour market including subsidising the semi-private salary insurance called _Dagpenge._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-9)

Income below [DKK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_krone "Danish krone") 50,543 (~US $8,300) (2021-level, adjusted annually) is income tax-free, but subject to the gross tax.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-limits-10)

The state (i.e., national) income tax has two income brackets (bottom and top).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-11) In 2016, around 10% of all tax payers had sufficiently high taxable incomes to be eligible for the top-bracket tax.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-skatter-12)

In 2023 the [Social Democratic-liberal coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederiksen_II_Cabinet "Frederiksen II Cabinet") of Prime Minister [Mette Frederiksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mette_Frederiksen "Mette Frederiksen") passed a tax reform that split the previous top-income tax bracket into three brackets:

*   First bracket: the so-called “Middle tax” (Danish: _mellemskat_) of an additional 7,5% on the margin levied on income between 618.400 and 750.000 DKK
*   Second bracket of 7,5% additional marginal tax levied on income between 750.000 and 2.5 million DKK
*   Third bracket: the so-called “Top-top tax” of an additional 5% marginal tax on income above 2.5 million DKK. However this has been criticized for being easily evadable by the individuals it is supposed to target

This tax reform is intended to increase long term labour supply,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-13) specifically in the light of the labour shortages experienced within various high skilled jobs, especially within fields like IT, engineering and health services[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-14)

There is also a municipal income tax varies from municipality to municipality, with rates varying from 22.5% to 27.8% in 2019.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-municip-15) Interest paid is deductible in the municipal tax. Interest expenses up to DKK 50,000 per individual (DKK 100,000 for couples) receive a further deduction of 8%. The great majority of tax payers have interest expenses below this threshold, implying that the tax value of interest expenditures for most tax payers is ca. 33%.

There exist a number of other important deductions in the municipal tax. Commuting exceeding 24 kilometres per day (15 mi/d) receives a DKK 1.98 per kilometre (DKK 3.19/mi) tax deduction. For most commutes exceeding 120 kilometres per day (75 mi/d), the rate is reduced to DKK 0.99 per kilometre (DKK 1.59/mi) above that threshold.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-16) A number of other deductions apply. Furthermore, union fees not exceeding DKK 6,000 annually are tax deductible as well as some other job-related expenses. Furthermore, most contributions to funded pension funds are deductible in both national and municipal taxes.

The sum of municipal and national tax percentages cannot exceed 52.05% (2019)–the so-called "tax ceiling" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _skatteloft_).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-17) Including the labour market contribution of 8%, the maximal effective marginal tax rate on labour income in 2019 is 55.9% (=0.08 + 0.92*0.5205). For capital income, there is a separate, lower maximum tax rate of 42% (Before inflation. Meaning real gains above inflation is effectively taxed higher than 42% because the tax is not adjusted for inflation).

#### Researcher Tax Scheme

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Researcher Tax Scheme")]

Certain people who have moved to Denmark to take up work as Researchers or Highly Paid Employees can become members of the Tax Scheme for Researchers. Members of the Scheme are exempt from normal taxation, but instead pay a 32.84% flat tax, inclusive of Labour market contributions.

Members of the Researcher Tax Scheme do not have tax cards as they are exempt and not part of the normal income tax system. They also do not pay Social Contributions or Municipal Taxes (except for taxes on wealth and property).

Members of the Scheme are only able to use it for taxes paid on their income at source, such as Payroll tax. If a member earns income that they have to report the tax on themselves (such as shares or at a side business) they have to pay tax on it through the normal system. When a member pays tax through the Researcher Scheme and through the normal taxation scheme the Government ignores their income from the Researcher Scheme when calculating their tax bands and tax rate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-18)

### Social Security Contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Social Security Contributions")]

There are also flat amounts in social contributions to particular funds in Denmark. These payments are set amounts in DKK, rather than a per cent of an individual's income. Both the employer and the employee are required by law to pay into these social funds, with the employee paying a total of DKK 1135 annually. ### Church tax

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Church tax")]

Members of the [Danish National Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_National_Church "Danish National Church") (about 75% of the Danish population) additionally pay an approximately 0.7% of their income to cover the expenditures of the National Church–the so-called [church tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_tax "Church tax") ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _kirkeskat_). The exact rate depends on the municipality. Whereas the collection of the church tax is administered by the Danish tax authorities and the tax rate is levied upon the same official income concept as the municipal tax, the church tax is not regarded as a proper tax by e.g. [Statistics Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Denmark "Statistics Denmark"), but as a "voluntary transfer from households to the state".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-19) One can be exempted from paying the church tax by opting out of being a member of the National Church.

### Tax on owner-occupied dwellings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tax on owner-occupied dwellings")]

In Denmark a special tax is levied upon the imputed income of owner-occupied dwellings. Its purpose is to create symmetry in the tax system by taxing the [imputed rent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imputed_rent "Imputed rent") of house owners. In 2019 the official tax rate is 1% (3% above a certain threshold) of the assessed value of the dwelling. However, the official assessment value is currently rather low compared to the average real market value of the dwellings. In 2017 the Danish parliament [Folketinget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folketinget "Folketinget") agreed upon a housing tax reform, according to which the effective tax rate from 2021 onward will be 0.44% (1.1% above a threshold) of a reformed and supposedly realistic assessment value.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-D%C3%98-20)

### Other income taxes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Other income taxes")]

The Danish corporate tax rate from 2016 onward is 22% of taxable corporate income, almost exactly equal to the average corporate income tax rate in all OECD countries in 2018.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-21) Personal income from shares (dividends as well as realized capital gains) are taxed at 27% below ca. DKK 50,000 and at 42% above the threshold.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-22)

The annual yields of most pension scheme assets is subject to a special tax of 15.3%. As assets in funded pension schemes make up a considerable part of national wealth in Denmark, this tax gives a considerable—and growing—revenue, amounting to DKK 32 billion in 2017 or around 3% of total tax revenues.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-skatter-12)

## Indirect taxation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Indirect taxation")]

The revenue from indirect taxes constituted around one third of the total Danish tax revenue in 2016.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-skatter-12) The single most important indirect tax as regards revenue is the Danish VAT, but Denmark also levies a land value tax on all privately owned land and a number of excise taxes.

### VAT

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: VAT")]

| Year | VAT level (Denmark) | Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1967 | 10% | MOMS |
| 1968 | 12.5% | MOMS |
| 1970 | 15% | MOMS |
| 1977 | 18% | MOMS |
| 1978 | 20.25% | MOMS |
| 1980 | 22% | MOMS |
| 1992 | 25% | MOMS |

Denmark has a non-deductible [value added tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_added_tax "Value added tax") (VAT) of 25% abbreviated as [[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-23) MOMS ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _merværdiafgift_, formerly _meromsætningsafgift_). The tax is subject to the [European Union value added tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_value_added_tax "European Union value added tax")[Directives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directive_(European_Union) "Directive (European Union)").

In Denmark, VAT is generally applied at one rate, and with few exceptions is not split into two or more rates as in other countries (e.g. Germany), where reduced rates apply to essential goods such as foodstuffs. A number of services are not subject to VAT, however, for instance public transportation of private persons, health care services, publishing newspapers, rent of premises (the lessor can, though, voluntarily register as VAT payer, except for residential premises), and travel agency operations.

### Land value tax

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Land value tax")]

The Danish grundskyld (part of the Municipal Property Tax) is a [land value tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_value_tax "Land value tax"), which taxes the base value of the land according to either:

*   The total value of the property minus the value of improvements or
*   The value of the property last tax year, altered by a growth/decline percentage.

Whichever of those two assessments is lower results in the base land value.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:5-25) This base land value is taxed at between 1.6 and 3.4% in 2019.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-municip-15) Agricultural land is taxed as well, but at lower rates.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-26)

### Registration fee on motorized vehicles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Registration fee on motorized vehicles")]

Like in Singapore, Brazil, and Norway, Denmark has a very high public taxation fee on buying motorized vehicles (cars, motorcycles, commercial vehicles). The motorized vehicle registration tax for private households is over 100% of approximately the first 100,000 DKK of the auto dealer's price, and 150% on the amounts over appr. 100.000 DKK of the auto dealer's price on the vehicle. Commercial enterprises and two-seater vehicles for private household buyers (no passenger seats in the back) pay a lower registration fee. An additional tax is required if commercial vehicles are used for private purposes. If this tax is not paid, and the vehicle is used privately, the tax penalty is severe.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-27)

## Denmark's tax structure in international comparison

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Denmark's tax structure in international comparison")]

The tax structure of Denmark (the relative weight of different taxes) differs from the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") average. In 2016, the Danish tax system was characterized by substantially higher revenues from taxes on personal income, whereas on the other hand, no revenues at all derive from social security contributions. A lower proportion of revenues in Denmark derive from taxes on corporate income and gains and property taxes than in OECD generally, whereas the proportion deriving from payroll taxes, VAT, and other taxes on goods and services correspond to the OECD average.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-28)

According to OECD, Denmark had the highest tax to GDP ratio of all its member countries in 2021 with a ratio of 47,4%.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-29) This is partly due to various tax-funded social transfer schemes such as pensions and unemployment benefits also being taxable when received by beneficiaries.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-31) Additionally, due to the Danish [universal welfare model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_welfare_state "Universal welfare state"), most Danish welfare schemes are tax funded as opposed to insurance-based, being calculated as a percentage of one's income tax instead of a lump sum contribution.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-32)

Professor of Economics at [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University")[Henrik Kleven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Kleven "Henrik Kleven") has suggested that three distinct principles of policies in Denmark and its Scandinavian neighbours imply that the high tax rates cause only relatively small distortions to the economy: widespread use of third-party information reporting for tax collection purposes (ensuring a low level of [tax evasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_evasion "Tax evasion")), broad [tax bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_base "Tax base") (ensuring a low level of [tax avoidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_avoidance "Tax avoidance")), and a strong subsidization of goods that are complementary to working (ensuring a high level of labour force participation).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-33)

**Taxation in Denmark** consists of a comprehensive system of direct and indirect taxes. Ever since the income tax was introduced in [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") via a fundamental tax reform in 1903, it has been a fundamental pillar in the Danish tax system. Today various personal and corporate income taxes yield around two thirds of the total Danish tax revenues, indirect taxes being responsible for the last third. The state personal income tax is a [progressive tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_tax "Progressive tax") while the municipal income tax is a [proportional tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_tax "Proportional tax") above a certain income level.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Overview")]

The types and levels of taxation in Denmark have changed dramatically since the state's inception. In the sixteenth century, Denmark primarily obtained state income through taxes excised on feudal [Demesne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demesne "Demesne") lands [[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:1-1) and the [Sound Dues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Dues "Sound Dues"), which required foreign ships to pay a toll when passing through the [Øresund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund "Øresund") bordering Denmark. In fact, the Dues comprised two-thirds of Denmark's tax revenue throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-2) The costs of warfare, such as those of the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War"), were further fulfilled by Denmark's heavily [agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture") economy. In later conflicts such as the [Scanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanian_War "Scanian War") and the [Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War "Great Northern War"), however, Denmark ceded much of its territory, resulting in monetary losses that prompted higher tax rates and the introduction of an initially small income tax. Massive population growth resulted in expansion of agriculture and consequently an expansion of taxes gained from tariffs on exports and wheat sales. By 1897, Denmark's income tax encompassed 15.00% [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) of the state's total revenue, far surpassing any other European country at the time. From 1897 to the present, Denmark continued to boast exceptionally high income tax rates, never dropping below the top five countries in Europe in terms of percentage revenue earned from income taxes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) Following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), as with many other countries, Denmark began to enact several social welfare programs, including aid for the sick and the unemployed.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:1-1) These, along with expansion of the [public sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_sector "Public sector") (schools, teachers, etc.) contributed to the income tax being a staple of Denmark's tax revenue.

### Changes in the 20th and 21st Centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Changes in the 20th and 21st Centuries")]

The exact form of income tax has varied through the past century. Between 1903 and 1966, income tax was levied only on "assessed" income, which did not include personal taxes that were spent on other areas, such as to the church. After 1966, income tax was changed to be levied on [taxable income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxable_income "Taxable income"), which included personal taxes spent on other areas and later also included income received from [stocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Share_capital "Share capital") and [interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest "Interest").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-4) In recent years, public sentiment[_[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No\_original\_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_] towards taxes has leaned towards limiting the [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state") and consequently the income tax. In 2001, a "tax freeze" that prevented the further increase of taxes was administered by the then liberal-conservative government of Denmark. The tax freeze could only be waived in particular times of crisis, and a tax could only be increased at the expense of a different form of tax.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-5) Furthermore, the Danish Tax Reform of 2010 gradually cut taxes "to increase labour supply in the medium to long term and at same time contribute to soften the effects of the global economic crises in the short run."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-6) The tax cuts impacted the high, middle, and low classes, and resulted in a net cut of 30 billion [DKK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_krone "Danish krone") between 2010 and 2019. Despite these policies, income taxes have stabilized at providing around 50% of Denmark's total revenue since 1990.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-:0-3) According to the [World Happiness Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Happiness_Report "World Happiness Report"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-7) Denmark ranks among the top two in terms of happiness, indicating a general contentedness with the state's welfare state and the benefits provided. The World Happiness Report also states that happiness is correlated to social equality. The official Denmark website remarks that "most Danes will tell you that they are happy to pay taxes because they can see what they get in return," including free tuition, healthcare, and social security.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-8)

### Municipal & National income tax

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Municipal & National income tax")]

All income from employment or self-employment is taxed at 8% before income tax. This tax is termed a "labour market contribution" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _arbejdsmarkedsbidrag_) or colloquially a "gross tax" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _bruttoskat_). The funds levied through this tax support the functions related to the labour market including subsidising the semi-private salary insurance called _Dagpenge._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-9)

Income below [DKK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_krone "Danish krone") 50,543 (~US $8,300) (2021-level, adjusted annually) is income tax-free, but subject to the gross tax.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-limits-10)

The state (i.e., national) income tax has two income brackets (bottom and top).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-11) In 2016, around 10% of all tax payers had sufficiently high taxable incomes to be eligible for the top-bracket tax.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-skatter-12)

In 2023 the [Social Democratic-liberal coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederiksen_II_Cabinet "Frederiksen II Cabinet") of Prime Minister [Mette Frederiksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mette_Frederiksen "Mette Frederiksen") passed a tax reform that split the previous top-income tax bracket into three brackets:

*   First bracket: the so-called “Middle tax” (Danish: _mellemskat_) of an additional 7,5% on the margin levied on income between 618.400 and 750.000 DKK
*   Second bracket of 7,5% additional marginal tax levied on income between 750.000 and 2.5 million DKK
*   Third bracket: the so-called “Top-top tax” of an additional 5% marginal tax on income above 2.5 million DKK. However this has been criticized for being easily evadable by the individuals it is supposed to target

This tax reform is intended to increase long term labour supply,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-13) specifically in the light of the labour shortages experienced within various high skilled jobs, especially within fields like IT, engineering and health services[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-14)

There is also a municipal income tax varies from municipality to municipality, with rates varying from 22.5% to 27.8% in 2019.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-municip-15) Interest paid is deductible in the municipal tax. Interest expenses up to DKK 50,000 per individual (DKK 100,000 for couples) receive a further deduction of 8%. The great majority of tax payers have interest expenses below this threshold, implying that the tax value of interest expenditures for most tax payers is ca. 33%.

There exist a number of other important deductions in the municipal tax. Commuting exceeding 24 kilometres per day (15 mi/d) receives a DKK 1.98 per kilometre (DKK 3.19/mi) tax deduction. For most commutes exceeding 120 kilometres per day (75 mi/d), the rate is reduced to DKK 0.99 per kilometre (DKK 1.59/mi) above that threshold.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-16) A number of other deductions apply. Furthermore, union fees not exceeding DKK 6,000 annually are tax deductible as well as some other job-related expenses. Furthermore, most contributions to funded pension funds are deductible in both national and municipal taxes.

The sum of municipal and national tax percentages cannot exceed 52.05% (2019)–the so-called "tax ceiling" ([Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_language "Danish language"): _skatteloft_).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-17) Including the labour market contribution of 8%, the maximal effective marginal tax rate on labour income in 2019 is 55.9% (=0.08 + 0.92*0.5205). For capital income, there is a separate, lower maximum tax rate of 42% (Before inflation. Meaning real gains above inflation is effectively taxed higher than 42% because the tax is not adjusted for inflation).

#### Researcher Tax Scheme

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Researcher Tax Scheme")]

Certain people who have moved to Denmark to take up work as Researchers or Highly Paid Employees can become members of the Tax Scheme for Researchers. Members of the Scheme are exempt from normal taxation, but instead pay a 32.84% flat tax, inclusive of Labour market contributions.

Members of the Researcher Tax Scheme do not have tax cards as they are exempt and not part of the normal income tax system. They also do not pay Social Contributions or Municipal Taxes (except for taxes on wealth and property).

Members of the Scheme are only able to use it for taxes paid on their income at source, such as Payroll tax. If a member earns income that they have to report the tax on themselves (such as shares or at a side business) they have to pay tax on it through the normal system. When a member pays tax through the Researcher Scheme and through the normal taxation scheme the Government ignores their income from the Researcher Scheme when calculating their tax bands and tax rate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_Denmark#cite_note-18)

### Social Security Contributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taxation_in_Denmark&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Social Security Contributions")]

There are also flat amounts in social contributions to particular funds in Denmark. These payments are set amounts in DKK, rather than a per cent of an individual's income. Both the employer and the employee are required by law to pay into these social funds, with the employee paying a total of DKK 1135 annually.
