Contents

Many of us want an overview of where our country stands on CO₂ and other greenhouse gas emissions. Are they increasing or decreasing? How do levels compare to other countries? This page provides the data for your chosen country across key metrics on this topic.

The data will be updated annually with the latest global and country emissions estimates.

[See all CO₂ & Greenhouse Gas Emissions data for Iceland](https://ourworldindata.org/search?countries=Iceland&topics=CO2+%26+Greenhouse+Gas+Emissions)

# How much CO₂ does Iceland emit per person?

In Iceland, CO₂ emissions per person were 9.67 tonnes in 2024.

Annual emissions figures are often used to compare countries’ contributions to climate change. But this metric often reflects differences in population size across the world.

To understand the ‘footprint’ of the average person in a given country, this chart shows per capita emissions. This is shown alongside countries with a similar level of income.

These figures reflect territorial emissions — emissions generated within a given country’s borders — so do not adjust for traded goods.

# [CO₂ emissions per capita](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co-emissions-per-capita?country=ISL~AND~NLD~FRO)
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from burning fossil fuels and industrial processes. This includes emissions from transport,electricity generation, and heating, but not land-use change.

# What are Iceland’s total annual emissions?

A country’s total contribution to climate change is obviously its footprint per person, multiplied by its population. This is what the chart here shows. Again, this is shown alongside countries with a similar level of income.

Iceland emitted 3.8 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2024.

These are territorial emissions, produced within the country’s borders. You will find consumption-based emissions, which adjust for imports and exports, later in this profile.

# What share of global CO₂ emissions are emitted by Iceland?

Looking at a country’s annual emissions is useful, but it can be hard to put these numbers in context. Is 10 million tonnes of CO 2 large or small? What about 100 million or 1 billion tonnes?

This interactive chart shows annual emissions as a percentage of the global total in a given year.

Iceland emitted <0.01% of the world’s CO 2 emissions in 2024.

# How much CO₂ has Iceland produced historically?

When we only look at emissions produced today, we lack context for historical responsibility for emissions over recent decades or centuries.

This interactive chart shows cumulative CO 2 emissions — the total emissions produced since 1751 up to the given year. This allows us to understand how much a given country has contributed to global emissions throughout its history. This is shown next to countries with a similar level of income today.

Iceland has emitted 172 million tonnes, as of 2024.

# What share of global historical CO₂ has Iceland emitted?

Just as with annual emissions, simply presenting cumulative CO 2 figures can be hard to contextualize. Has a given country’s contribution to the global total been large or small?

This chart shows the country’s cumulative emissions as a share of global cumulative emissions.

Iceland has emitted <0.01% of global CO 2 emissions since 1751.

# What share of Iceland’s CO₂ emissions are produced from different fuels?

CO 2 emissions are dominated by the burning of fossil fuels for energy production, and industrial production of materials such as cement.

What is the contribution of each fuel source to the country’s CO 2 emissions?

This interactive chart shows the breakdown of annual CO 2 emissions by source: either coal, oil, gas, cement production or gas flaring. This breakdown is strongly influenced by a country's energy mix and changes as it shifts to or away from a given energy source.

# How are Iceland’s CO₂ emissions from different fuels changing?

The chart above allows us to see the breakdown of CO 2 emissions by fuel type. But it makes it more difficult to see the absolute change in particular fuel sources over time.

This interactive chart shows the same data — CO 2 emissions from coal, oil, gas, cement and flaring — but as individual lines to see clearly how each is changing over time.

# How much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

The charts above focused on carbon dioxide (CO 2). But CO 2 is not the only greenhouse gas. Others, including methane and nitrous oxide, have also had a significant impact on global warming to date.

The first interactive chart shows per capita greenhouse gas emissions. This is measured as the sum of all greenhouse gases, and given by a metric called ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

‘Carbon dioxide equivalents’ try to correct for the fact that one unit (e.g. a tonne) of a given gas doesn’t have the same impact on warming as another. We therefore multiply the emissions of each gas by its ‘global warming potential’ (GWP) value: this measures the amount of warming one tonne of that gas would create relative to one tonne of CO 2.

In 2024, the average person in Iceland emitted 12.9 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO 2 eq).

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

# Methane: how much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

Methane (CH 4) is a strong greenhouse gas, mainly produced through agricultural activities (e.g. livestock and rice production), in addition to leakages from oil and gas production (called ‘fugitive emissions’).

This first interactive chart here shows per capita emissions of methane each year. This is measured in ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

Emissions from fossil fuels, industry, agriculture, and land-use change are included.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/methane-emissions?country=ISL)

# Nitrous oxide: how much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is a strong greenhouse gas that is mainly produced from agricultural activities (e.g. from the use of synthetic and organic fertilizers to grow crops).

This first interactive chart here shows per capita emissions of nitrous oxide each year. This is measured in ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

# Energy intensity: how much energy does Iceland use per unit of GDP?

Energy is a large contributor to CO 2 emissions, but it also matters for human development and rising living standards.

Energy intensity can therefore be a useful metric to monitor. Energy intensity measures the amount of energy consumed per unit of gross domestic product. It effectively measures how efficiently a country uses energy to produce a given amount of economic output. A lower energy intensity means it needs less energy per unit of GDP.

This interactive chart shows energy intensity, alongside countries with a similar level of income.

In 2022, Iceland used 5.35 kWh of energy per unit of GDP.

# Carbon intensity: how much carbon does Iceland emit per unit of energy?

Energy intensity — shown in the chart above — is an important metric for monitoring whether countries are making progress in reducing emissions. Another is carbon intensity: the amount of CO 2 emitted per unit of energy.

As we transition our energy mix towards lower-carbon sources (such as renewables or nuclear energy), the amount of carbon we emit per unit of energy should fall.

This chart shows carbon intensity.

In 2024, Iceland emitted 43.89 kilograms of CO 2 per kilowatt-hour.

# Has Iceland’s economic growth decoupled from its CO₂ emissions?

To reduce emissions and achieve increasing prosperity at the same time, we have to decouple economic growth from CO 2 emissions. [Several countries](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/consumption-co2-per-capita-vs-gdppc?zoomToSelection=true&endpointsOnly=1&time=1990..2016&country=BGR~CYP~CZE~DNK~EST~FIN~FRA~DEU~GRC~HUN~ITA~LVA~LTU~NLD~POL~PRT~ROU~SVK~ESP~SWE~GBR~ISR~JOR~ARM) have achieved this in recent years.

The chart here shows whether this country has achieved this by showing the change in GDP per capita, and annual per capita CO 2 emissions over time.

We show both territorial and consumption-based emissions (where available). This allows us to see whether the import of production from other countries — or the export to other countries — has affected this change in emissions.

Contents

Many of us want an overview of where our country stands on CO₂ and other greenhouse gas emissions. Are they increasing or decreasing? How do levels compare to other countries? This page provides the data for your chosen country across key metrics on this topic.

The data will be updated annually with the latest global and country emissions estimates.

# How much CO₂ does Iceland emit per person?

In Iceland, CO₂ emissions per person were 9.67 tonnes in 2024.

Annual emissions figures are often used to compare countries’ contributions to climate change. But this metric often reflects differences in population size across the world.

To understand the ‘footprint’ of the average person in a given country, this chart shows per capita emissions. This is shown alongside countries with a similar level of income.

These figures reflect territorial emissions — emissions generated within a given country’s borders — so do not adjust for traded goods.

# [CO₂ emissions per capita](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co-emissions-per-capita?country=ISL~AND~NLD~FRO)
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from burning fossil fuels and industrial processes. This includes emissions from transport,electricity generation, and heating, but not land-use change.

# What are Iceland’s total annual emissions?

A country’s total contribution to climate change is obviously its footprint per person, multiplied by its population. This is what the chart here shows. Again, this is shown alongside countries with a similar level of income.

Iceland emitted 3.8 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2024.

These are territorial emissions, produced within the country’s borders. You will find consumption-based emissions, which adjust for imports and exports, later in this profile.

# What share of global CO₂ emissions are emitted by Iceland?

Looking at a country’s annual emissions is useful, but it can be hard to put these numbers in context. Is 10 million tonnes of CO 2 large or small? What about 100 million or 1 billion tonnes?

This interactive chart shows annual emissions as a percentage of the global total in a given year.

Iceland emitted <0.01% of the world’s CO 2 emissions in 2024.

# How much CO₂ has Iceland produced historically?

When we only look at emissions produced today, we lack context for historical responsibility for emissions over recent decades or centuries.

This interactive chart shows cumulative CO 2 emissions — the total emissions produced since 1751 up to the given year. This allows us to understand how much a given country has contributed to global emissions throughout its history. This is shown next to countries with a similar level of income today.

Iceland has emitted 172 million tonnes, as of 2024.

# What share of global historical CO₂ has Iceland emitted?

Just as with annual emissions, simply presenting cumulative CO 2 figures can be hard to contextualize. Has a given country’s contribution to the global total been large or small?

This chart shows the country’s cumulative emissions as a share of global cumulative emissions.

Iceland has emitted <0.01% of global CO 2 emissions since 1751.

# What share of Iceland’s CO₂ emissions are produced from different fuels?

CO 2 emissions are dominated by the burning of fossil fuels for energy production, and industrial production of materials such as cement.

What is the contribution of each fuel source to the country’s CO 2 emissions?

This interactive chart shows the breakdown of annual CO 2 emissions by source: either coal, oil, gas, cement production or gas flaring. This breakdown is strongly influenced by a country's energy mix and changes as it shifts to or away from a given energy source.

# How are Iceland’s CO₂ emissions from different fuels changing?

The chart above allows us to see the breakdown of CO 2 emissions by fuel type. But it makes it more difficult to see the absolute change in particular fuel sources over time.

This interactive chart shows the same data — CO 2 emissions from coal, oil, gas, cement and flaring — but as individual lines to see clearly how each is changing over time.

# How much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

The charts above focused on carbon dioxide (CO 2). But CO 2 is not the only greenhouse gas. Others, including methane and nitrous oxide, have also had a significant impact on global warming to date.

The first interactive chart shows per capita greenhouse gas emissions. This is measured as the sum of all greenhouse gases, and given by a metric called ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

‘Carbon dioxide equivalents’ try to correct for the fact that one unit (e.g. a tonne) of a given gas doesn’t have the same impact on warming as another. We therefore multiply the emissions of each gas by its ‘global warming potential’ (GWP) value: this measures the amount of warming one tonne of that gas would create relative to one tonne of CO 2.

In 2024, the average person in Iceland emitted 12.9 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO 2 eq).

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

# Methane: how much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

Methane (CH 4) is a strong greenhouse gas, mainly produced through agricultural activities (e.g. livestock and rice production), in addition to leakages from oil and gas production (called ‘fugitive emissions’).

This first interactive chart here shows per capita emissions of methane each year. This is measured in ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

Emissions from fossil fuels, industry, agriculture, and land-use change are included.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/methane-emissions?country=ISL)

# Nitrous oxide: how much does the average person in Iceland emit? Where do emissions come from?

Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is a strong greenhouse gas that is mainly produced from agricultural activities (e.g. from the use of synthetic and organic fertilizers to grow crops).

This first interactive chart here shows per capita emissions of nitrous oxide each year. This is measured in ‘carbon dioxide equivalents’.

The other interactive chart shows the sources of these emissions and the contribution of each sector.

# Energy intensity: how much energy does Iceland use per unit of GDP?

Energy is a large contributor to CO 2 emissions, but it also matters for human development and rising living standards.

Energy intensity can therefore be a useful metric to monitor. Energy intensity measures the amount of energy consumed per unit of gross domestic product. It effectively measures how efficiently a country uses energy to produce a given amount of economic output. A lower energy intensity means it needs less energy per unit of GDP.

This interactive chart shows energy intensity, alongside countries with a similar level of income.

In 2022, Iceland used 5.35 kWh of energy per unit of GDP.

# Carbon intensity: how much carbon does Iceland emit per unit of energy?

Energy intensity — shown in the chart above — is an important metric for monitoring whether countries are making progress in reducing emissions. Another is carbon intensity: the amount of CO 2 emitted per unit of energy.

As we transition our energy mix towards lower-carbon sources (such as renewables or nuclear energy), the amount of carbon we emit per unit of energy should fall.

This chart shows carbon intensity.

In 2024, Iceland emitted 43.89 kilograms of CO 2 per kilowatt-hour.

# Has Iceland’s economic growth decoupled from its CO₂ emissions?

To reduce emissions and achieve increasing prosperity at the same time, we have to decouple economic growth from CO 2 emissions. [Several countries](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/consumption-co2-per-capita-vs-gdppc?zoomToSelection=true&endpointsOnly=1&time=1990..2016&country=BGR~CYP~CZE~DNK~EST~FIN~FRA~DEU~GRC~HUN~ITA~LVA~LTU~NLD~POL~PRT~ROU~SVK~ESP~SWE~GBR~ISR~JOR~ARM) have achieved this in recent years.

The chart here shows whether this country has achieved this by showing the change in GDP per capita, and annual per capita CO 2 emissions over time.

We show both territorial and consumption-based emissions (where available). This allows us to see whether the import of production from other countries — or the export to other countries — has affected this change in emissions.

# Iceland With Highest Per Capita Emissions In Europe

Aug 20, 2021

/

[News](https://grapevine.is/news/)

Words by 

[Andie Sophia Fontaine](https://grapevine.is/author/andie-fontaine/ "Posts by Andie Sophia Fontaine")

Photo by Brilliantwiki/Wikimedia Commons

New [data](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/-/ddn-20210818-1) from Eurostat shows Iceland to be the largest polluter when it comes to net emissions of greenhouse gases in Europe, in terms of tonnes per capita. However, some sectors are more polluting than others.

The European Union average shows 7.8 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions per capita. In Iceland, that average is 40.9 tonnes. Sweden ranked lowest, at 1.8 tonnes, while the second-highest was Luxembourg, at 19.7 tonnes.

That said, “per capita” is of course just an average; different sectors of Icelandic society pollute more than others.

[RÚV](https://www.ruv.is/frett/2021/08/20/island-enn-langefst-a-lista-yfir-losun-a-hvern-ibua) reports that the biggest polluter in Iceland is in land use. Data from [2019](https://grapevine.is/news/2019/04/16/icelands-greenhouse-gas-emissions-increase/) also shows that local transport, fishing vessels, industrial livestock farming and landfills also contribute heavily.

Emissions from heavy industry have increased by 133% since 1990, and emissions from car traffic have increased by 85% since 1990 and by 5.5% between 2016 and 2017. A report from the Environment Agency of Iceland found in 2019 that emissions were also exacerbated by the increase of tourism, due to both a sharp increase in both rented vehicles and flights to and from Iceland.

All this being the case, while the statistical average is troubling, the average individual Icelander is not releasing 40.9 tonnes of greenhouse gases; a few sectors that are in large part under the auspices of the Icelandic government are.

# Iceland With Highest Per Capita Emissions In Europe

Aug 20, 2021

/

[News](https://grapevine.is/news/)

Words by 

[Andie Sophia Fontaine](https://grapevine.is/author/andie-fontaine/ "Posts by Andie Sophia Fontaine")

Photo by Brilliantwiki/Wikimedia Commons

New [data](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/-/ddn-20210818-1) from Eurostat shows Iceland to be the largest polluter when it comes to net emissions of greenhouse gases in Europe, in terms of tonnes per capita. However, some sectors are more polluting than others.

The European Union average shows 7.8 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions per capita. In Iceland, that average is 40.9 tonnes. Sweden ranked lowest, at 1.8 tonnes, while the second-highest was Luxembourg, at 19.7 tonnes.

That said, “per capita” is of course just an average; different sectors of Icelandic society pollute more than others.

[RÚV](https://www.ruv.is/frett/2021/08/20/island-enn-langefst-a-lista-yfir-losun-a-hvern-ibua) reports that the biggest polluter in Iceland is in land use. Data from [2019](https://grapevine.is/news/2019/04/16/icelands-greenhouse-gas-emissions-increase/) also shows that local transport, fishing vessels, industrial livestock farming and landfills also contribute heavily.

Emissions from heavy industry have increased by 133% since 1990, and emissions from car traffic have increased by 85% since 1990 and by 5.5% between 2016 and 2017. A report from the Environment Agency of Iceland found in 2019 that emissions were also exacerbated by the increase of tourism, due to both a sharp increase in both rented vehicles and flights to and from Iceland.

All this being the case, while the statistical average is troubling, the average individual Icelander is not releasing 40.9 tonnes of greenhouse gases; a few sectors that are in large part under the auspices of the Icelandic government are.

Abstract. Environmental problems mitigation and the transition towards a
greener  economy  with  the  objective  of  becoming  climate  neutral  is  made
possible  through  environmental  regulations.  Environmental  taxes  can  be
considered  one  of  the  best  instruments  needed  when  elaborating  and
implementing environmental protection policies, especially because they act
as vectors of change that can ensure achieving the sustainable development
goals. On the other hand, greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere rose
to new records in 2019 and act as obstacles in becoming climate neutral and
achieving the Goal 13 of sustainable development, the latter addressing the
urgent  need  to  adopt  measures  meant  to  combat  climate  change  and  its
impact,  therefore  measures  designed  to  de-carbonize  economic  activities,
especially  in  countries  with  higher  emissions  of  greenhouse  gases.  In  this
context, the main objective undertook in this research paper was to estimate
the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues  based  on  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in the case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Results highlight strong correlations and statistically significant between the
amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  two  types  of  environmental  tax
revenues:  energy  and  transport.  The  linear  cross–sectional  econometric
methodology (least-squares method) was applied to the data referring to the
year 2018. However, results point to the fact that the only valid econometric
model  constructed  is  the  one  estimating  the  transport  environmental  tax
revenues based on the levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

Introduction
In  a  global  context  marked  by  the  green  development
movement,  environmental  tax  revenues  represent  one  of  the  main
sources  to  generate  public  revenue  in  the  spirit  of  bringing
environmental  issues  to  the  attention  of  citizens.  In  contemporary
economies,  environmental  taxation  represents  a  key  tool  for
promoting  environmentally  friendly  technologies,  but,  above  all,
environmental taxation shapes responsible behaviors and consolidates
specific  dedicated  policies  (Dinu  et  al.,  2020),  especially  taking  into
account the negative effects of phenomena such as biodiversity loss,
degradation of ecosystems and the more sensitive air pollution. In this
context, environmental tax revenues represents a relevant indicator for
understanding specific environmental policies. Not only that, but also
environmental  tax  revenues  aim  at  mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful
actions  against  the  environment  in  a  resource-efficient  manner.
Economic instruments for pollution control and efficient management
of  natural  resources  represent  an  essential  part  in  the  case  of  the
environmental and energy policies in the European Union.
Environmental  tax  revenues  can  be  used  to  address
environmental  issues,  such  as:  poor  waste  disposal,  high  levels  of
pollution  of  any  kind:  water,  air,  soil,  and  other  forms  of
environmental  issues.  In  this  context,  as  is  argues  in  numerous
literature  (Villar‐Rubio  &  Huete‐Morales,  2017;  Andreoni,  2019;
Torney, 2019; Cadoret et al., 2020), no matter the nature of policies
which  imply  designing  and  implementing  measures  specific  to
resorting to environmental tax revenues – all these policies are highly
depended  on  their  socio-economic  substantiation.  Moreover,  one  of
the  instruments  used  to  influence  the  economic  behaviors  of
consumers  and  producers  towards  sustainability  has  been  the
environmental  tax  revenues  –  a  flexible  cost-effective  manner  for
harnessing the polluter-pays principle among the European citizens.
As it is shown in (European Commission, 2019a), during 2018,
the  governments  of  countries  part  of  the  European  Union  collected
324.6  billion  €  of  environmental  tax  revenues,  representing  2.4%  of

the European Union’s GDP and 6.0% of the total government revenue
coming from social contributions and taxes.
As referring to its distribution, according to the calculus based
on Eurostat, (2020) and European Commission, (2019a), nevertheless,
approximately  78%  of  the  total  environmental  tax  revenues  comes
from the energy sector, approximately 19% represents transport taxes,
and  the  rest  (approximately  3%)  comes  from  taxes  on  pollution and
resources,  therefore  the  latter  having  a  small  share  out  of  the  total
taxes.
According  to  (European  Commission,  2019),  the  European
Green  Deal  is  ensuring  that  taxation  is  aligned  with  the  objectives
specific  to  climate  change  is essential  and  delivering  the  European
Green Deal can be made possible only by rethinking national budgets
as the means of the transition for a cleaner European economy – and
not  only.  Better  management  of  green  budgeting  instruments  will
contribute  to  redirecting  consumption  behaviors,  production  patterns
and taxation to green priorities in the European Union. The transition
to  the  green  circular  economy  –  sustainable  in  terms  of  resource
allocation, availability and use, it calls for the implementation of more
efficient  and  environmentally  responsible  taxation  frameworks.  This
green  transition  requires  both  the  modernization  of  environmental
taxation systems and the expansion of opportunities for promoting and
implementing clean, environmentally friendly technologies  – capable
of generating higher levels of added-value, therefore technologies that
are economically competitive on global markets.
Environmental policies also involve frameworks and actions in
relation  to  climate  change  strategies  and  such  policies  have  a
significant fiscal component. The latter is  based on a comprehensive
sanction  mechanism  –  compensation  specific  to  environmental
taxation. From this perspective, a relevant example is that through the
new  Circular  Economy  Action  Plan  for  a  cleaner  and  more
competitive Europe (European Commission, 2020), among others, the
European  Union  aims  at  ―achieving  climate  neutrality  by  2050  and
decoupling economic growth from resource use‖. In order to ensure a
climate-neutral, circular and resource-efficient economy, the European
Commission will propose policies that can also include references to
environmental taxes – as means of achieving climate neutrality.

According  to  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambitions  (European
Commission, 2020), the greenhouse  gas emissions are to be reduced
of at least 55% by 2030 compared to the year 1990, as it is considered
to improve the wellbeing of EU citizens and to support the COVID-19
recovery,  along  with  the  resilience  and  competitiveness  of  the
European  economy.  In  this  context,  the  EU  taxonomy  will  be  an
essential  instrument  to  bring  finance  closer  to  the  needs  of  the
transition to a cleaner economy. Since it is argued that high levels of
environmental tax revenues can contribute to raising the quality of the
environment  and  environmental  protection  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-
Chudzio,  2017) and  taking  into  consideration  the  importance  for  the
EU  members  to  facilitate  the  transition  to  a  circular  and  climate-
neutral  economy  through  EU  taxonomy,  the  main  objective  of  this
research  was  to  design  a  cross–sectional  linear  regression  model
meant  to  estimate  the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues
structurally based on the  amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the
case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the
year 2018 as the reference point for this study.

Literature review
In  the  European  Union,  the  evolution  of  environmental  tax
revenues is grounded in the historical heritage of each country and it is
influenced by socio-economic aspects such as the degree of economic
development,  size  of  the  population,  consumption  and  production
behaviors and other factors (Štreimikienė, 2015).
Through  environmental  tax  revenues,  the  European  Union
member  states  provide  disincentives  to  consumption  and  build
towards  a  more  green,  environmentally-friendly  economic
development  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-Chudzio,  2019). European  states
which  have  implemented  reforms  concerning  the  topic  of
environmental  tax  revenues  have  achieved  their  socio-economic  and
environmental  objectives  more  efficiently  than  those  who  did  not
focus,  for  various  reasons,  on  elaborating  and  implementing  well-
thought  environmental  tax  collecting  reforms  (Miceikiene  et  al.,
2016).
However, this is not only the case of the European Union. Fan,
Li  and  Yin  (2019)  mathematically  confirmed  that  imposing

pp. 45  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 5]
environmental  tax  significantly  contributes  to  achieving  green
development, based on a small set of data referring to China. On the
other  hand,  Still,  Piciu,  Ipate  and  Bogdan  (2016)  argue  that
environmental  taxes  should  not  only  act  as  a  tool  for  building  a
cleaner economy, but rather it must also contribute to obtaining a fair
market  price,  in  consonance  with  both  the  results  coming  from  the
economic scientific research teams and from the political will.
Tantau, Maassen and Fratila (2018) designed a panel regression model
meant  to  determine  the  dependency  between  indicators  that  assess
progress  of  the  circular  economy  in  Europe.  In  the  constructed
econometric model, the authors included environmental tax revenues
as  one  of  the  main  independent  variables,  which  proved  to  be
significant  within  the  regression  model  in  relation  to  the  rest  of  the
independent variables and in relation to the dependent variable – the
recycling rate of municipal waste, at the level of the EU-28 members,
corresponding to the 2010-2014 period.
An econometric study carried out at the level of the European
Union level concerning the 2010-2017 period highlights how strategic
and  careful  socio-economic  and  ecological  policies  must  be
constructed,  since  an  increase  of  the  expenses  concerning
environmental  taxes  could  eventually  act  as  an  impediment  for
potential investors in future ecological projects (Banacu et al., 2019),
even  though  taxes  would  initially  be  designed  to  harness  the
implementation of green initiatives.
Through a panel smooth transition regression approach, Cepoi,
Bran  and  Dinu  (2020)  suggest  that  European  countries  should
implement measures designed to avoid environmental degradation by
intensifying the use of biofuels and not only relying on environmental
taxes.
Chu,  Cheng  and  Lai  (2018)  proved  the  importance  of  the
distribution  of  environmental  tax  revenues  per  generations.  They
demonstrated  that  this  form  of  tax  revenues  must  be  considered
according  to  the  needs  and  possibilities  of  both  the  young  and  old
generations. The authors argue that raising environmental taxes could
potentially  generate  inter-generational  conflicts  concerning  the
environmental policy and that would be undesirable considering that
there are ways to appropriately establish thresholds for environmental

taxes in such a manner that can assure the long-term improvement of
welfare of all generations.
Merko,  Dursun  and  Merko  (2018)  demonstrated  that  the
environmental tax revenues represent an important share of Albania’s
GDP  (2.77%  on  average)  and  that  this  form  of  revenues  is
characterized  by  an  average  increase  of  4.7%  in  the  same  analyzed
period, 2008-2015. The greatest share of environmental tax revenues
was registered in the case of the energy sector (56.64%).
In other study, Miceikiene  and Ciuleviciene (2016)  identified
some of the factors that influence the environmental tax revenues and
some  of  those  are  the  following:  nominal  GDP,  energy  saving,
municipality-generated  waste, renewable energy production, nominal
environmental protection expenditure and others. Moreover, the same
authors argue that the nominal GDP has the most impactful influence
on the variation of the environmental tax revenues in Lithuania.
However,  other  authors  (Leibus  and  Mazure,  2016)
demonstrated  that  environmental  tax  revenues  have  relatively  small
shares  in  the  case  of  the  Baltic  States.  Considering  the  1994-2012
timeframe  and  the  European  countries  included  in  the  OECD
database,  a  study  (Onofrei  et  al.,  2017)  based  on  panel  data  fixed-
effect estimation techniques empirically proved that environmental tax
revenues  represent  an  important  vector  designed  to  reduce  pollution
levels,  especially  when  approached  in  relation  to  the  generation  of
greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Speck  (2017)  argues  that  decreasing
greenhouse  gas  emissions  in  the  European  Union  by  80-95%  by  the
year 2050 reported to the 1990 year levels will determine a decrease
of the tax base of both the energy taxes and carbon pricing.

included  in  this  study  are  (i)  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  (ii)
environmental  tax  revenues,  split  per  component  (energy,  transport
and pollution & resources) – as included in Table 1.

Data  regarding  the  indicators  included  in  Table  1  were  taken  over

The  greenhouse  gas  emissions  indicator  is  part  of  the  EU
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDG)  designed  to  assess  progress
towards  Goal  13  on  climate  action.  Part  of  the  2030  Agenda  for
Sustainable  Development  (United  Nations,  2015),  SDG  13  aims  to
implement  the  commitment  to  climate  change objectives  and  reduce
the  amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Such  measures  are
furthermore  encouraged  by  the  European  Green  Deal,  Circular
Economy  Action  Plan  and  part  of  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambition.
The indicator quantifies total national emissions, international aviation
included. Gases include carbon  dioxide,  methane,  nitrous  oxide,  and
F-gases. Using the individual global warming potential of each of the
gases, they are expressed in units of carbon dioxide equivalents.
As described by Eurostat (2020), environmental  tax revenues
are  part  of  the  environmental  accounts  that  constitute  a  satellite
account  to  national  accounts.  This  indicator  is  split  per  category,  as
described in Table 1. Eurostat considers an environmental tax any tax
whose  base  is  a  physical  unit  of  actions  that  has  a  proven  negative
impact on the natural capital. In order for payments to be identified as
environmental taxes, they must be tracked in the national accounts as
environmental taxes. Other forms of payments to government are not
considered  revenues based on environmental taxes. It is important to

The  research  method  used  in  this  study  is  econometric.
Multiple  cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  designed  in
order  to  find  the  best  model  for  estimating  the  amount  of
environmental tax revenues (i.e.: best tax revenue category), based on
the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  generated  by  the  selected  European
countries included in this study. In all of the constructed econometric
models,  the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  represent  the  independent
variable  and  the  environmental  tax  revenues  (split  per  category)
represent the dependent variable. This research method is quantitative,
based  on  cross–sectional  statistic  data,  characterized  by  multiple
observations studied at a single moment in time (the year 2018 in this
particular  research),  referring  to  multiple  entities  (i.e.:  European
countries).

The Student-t values of the parameters are calculated in the
t–Statistic  column.  In  order  to  validate  all  the  environmental  tax
revenues  structural  estimation  models  in  relation  to  the  greenhouse
gas emissions, the Prob. values need to be minimum, ideally zero, so
that the parameters of the variables significantly differ from zero. This
is only the case for the model which estimates transport environmental
tax revenues based on the greenhouse gas emissions.
R2  indicates  that  58.90%  of  the  variation  of  the  transport
environmental  tax  revenues  is  explained  by  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in 2018 in the case of the analyzed European countries. In
order  to  mitigate  the  mechanical  increase  in  the  coefficient  of
determination, Adjusted R2 validates the model, considering that there
is a drop only from 58.90% to 57.48% between R2 and the Adjusted
R2.
Considering the equation of the econometric model, should the
greenhouse gas emissions in any of the analyzed European countries
be situated around the mean, 130.33 million tonnes for example, then
it  is estimated  that  the  transport  environmental  tax  revenues  in  that
respective  country  will  be  2,643.77  million  EUR  (calculated:
748.1074 + (14.5451 × 130.33)).

Conclusion
The  transition  towards  a  greener  circular  economy  with  the
goal  of becoming  climate neutral is made possible, among other, by
resorting  to  an  important  instrument:  environmental  regulations and,
more  specifically,  environmental  tax  revenues.  The  latter  aim  at
mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful  actions  against  the  environment  in
resources-efficient manners, especially in the European Union.
In  the  case  of  the  analyzed  European  countries,  the  energy
sector  represents  the  major  source  of  environmental  pollution  and,
consequently,  a  corresponding  high  level  of  environmental  tax
revenues.  In  2018,  the  governments  of  the  members  part  of  the
European  Union  collected  324.6  billions  €  of  environmental  tax
revenues, representing 2.4% of the European Union’s GDP.
The environment tax proves to be a real policy instrument for
green development. The European Green Deal ensures that taxation is
aligned  with  the  objectives  specific  to  climate  change.  The  2030
Agenda for Sustainable  Development aims at decreasing the  amount
of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  this  can  be  made  possible  through
environmental taxes, grounded on the polluter-pays principle.
The main objective of this research was achieved, as multiple
cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  constructed  with  the
aim to estimate the amount of environmental tax revenues structurally
based on the amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the case of EU
members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the year 2018
as  the  reference  point  for  this  study. Results  highlight  that  the  only
valid econometric model is that in the case of transport environmental
tax revenues estimated in relation with the generated greenhouse gas
emissions.  The  model  proves  that  one  additional  million  tonne  of

14.5451 million EUR of transport environmental taxes, at the level of
the year 2018, in the case of the analyzed European countries.
The  main  limitation  of  this  study  refers  to  the  fact  that  the
analysis does not encompass historic data of the studied phenomena.
However, this study can be extended by approaching the same subject
in  a  different  manner  –  considering  a  panel  data  approach  and  even

Abstract. Environmental problems mitigation and the transition towards a
greener  economy  with  the  objective  of  becoming  climate  neutral  is  made
possible  through  environmental  regulations.  Environmental  taxes  can  be
considered  one  of  the  best  instruments  needed  when  elaborating  and
implementing environmental protection policies, especially because they act
as vectors of change that can ensure achieving the sustainable development
goals. On the other hand, greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere rose
to new records in 2019 and act as obstacles in becoming climate neutral and
achieving the Goal 13 of sustainable development, the latter addressing the
urgent  need  to  adopt  measures  meant  to  combat  climate  change  and  its
impact,  therefore  measures  designed  to  de-carbonize  economic  activities,
especially  in  countries  with  higher  emissions  of  greenhouse  gases.  In  this
context, the main objective undertook in this research paper was to estimate
the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues  based  on  the  greenhouse  gas
emissions in the case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Results highlight strong correlations and statistically significant between the
amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  two  types  of  environmental  tax
revenues:  energy  and  transport.  The  linear  cross–sectional  econometric
methodology (least-squares method) was applied to the data referring to the
year 2018. However, results point to the fact that the only valid econometric
model  constructed  is  the  one  estimating  the  transport  environmental  tax
revenues based on the levels of greenhouse gas emissions.

Introduction
In  a  global  context  marked  by  the  green  development
movement,  environmental  tax  revenues  represent  one  of  the  main
sources  to  generate  public  revenue  in  the  spirit  of  bringing
environmental  issues  to  the  attention  of  citizens.  In  contemporary
economies,  environmental  taxation  represents  a  key  tool  for
promoting  environmentally  friendly  technologies,  but,  above  all,
environmental taxation shapes responsible behaviors and consolidates
specific  dedicated  policies  (Dinu  et  al.,  2020),  especially  taking  into
account the negative effects of phenomena such as biodiversity loss,
degradation of ecosystems and the more sensitive air pollution. In this
context, environmental tax revenues represents a relevant indicator for
understanding specific environmental policies. Not only that, but also
environmental  tax  revenues  aim  at  mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful
actions  against  the  environment  in  a  resource-efficient  manner.
Economic instruments for pollution control and efficient management
of  natural  resources  represent  an  essential  part  in  the  case  of  the
environmental and energy policies in the European Union.
Environmental  tax  revenues  can  be  used  to  address
environmental  issues,  such  as:  poor  waste  disposal,  high  levels  of
pollution  of  any  kind:  water,  air,  soil,  and  other  forms  of
environmental  issues.  In  this  context,  as  is  argues  in  numerous
literature  (Villar‐Rubio  &  Huete‐Morales,  2017;  Andreoni,  2019;
Torney, 2019; Cadoret et al., 2020), no matter the nature of policies
which  imply  designing  and  implementing  measures  specific  to
resorting to environmental tax revenues – all these policies are highly
depended  on  their  socio-economic  substantiation.  Moreover,  one  of
the  instruments  used  to  influence  the  economic  behaviors  of
consumers  and  producers  towards  sustainability  has  been  the
environmental  tax  revenues  –  a  flexible  cost-effective  manner  for
harnessing the polluter-pays principle among the European citizens.
As it is shown in (European Commission, 2019a), during 2018,
the  governments  of  countries  part  of  the  European  Union  collected
324.6  billion  €  of  environmental  tax  revenues,  representing  2.4%  of

DOI: 10.2478/9788366675261-004
pp. 43  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 3]
the European Union’s GDP and 6.0% of the total government revenue
coming from social contributions and taxes.
As referring to its distribution, according to the calculus based
on Eurostat, (2020) and European Commission, (2019a), nevertheless,
approximately  78%  of  the  total  environmental  tax  revenues  comes
from the energy sector, approximately 19% represents transport taxes,
and  the  rest  (approximately  3%)  comes  from  taxes  on  pollution and
resources,  therefore  the  latter  having  a  small  share  out  of  the  total
taxes.
According  to  (European  Commission,  2019),  the  European
Green  Deal  is  ensuring  that  taxation  is  aligned  with  the  objectives
specific  to  climate  change  is essential  and  delivering  the  European
Green Deal can be made possible only by rethinking national budgets
as the means of the transition for a cleaner European economy – and
not  only.  Better  management  of  green  budgeting  instruments  will
contribute  to  redirecting  consumption  behaviors,  production  patterns
and taxation to green priorities in the European Union. The transition
to  the  green  circular  economy  –  sustainable  in  terms  of  resource
allocation, availability and use, it calls for the implementation of more
efficient  and  environmentally  responsible  taxation  frameworks.  This
green  transition  requires  both  the  modernization  of  environmental
taxation systems and the expansion of opportunities for promoting and
implementing clean, environmentally friendly technologies  – capable
of generating higher levels of added-value, therefore technologies that
are economically competitive on global markets.
Environmental policies also involve frameworks and actions in
relation  to  climate  change  strategies  and  such  policies  have  a
significant fiscal component. The latter is  based on a comprehensive
sanction  mechanism  –  compensation  specific  to  environmental
taxation. From this perspective, a relevant example is that through the
new  Circular  Economy  Action  Plan  for  a  cleaner  and  more
competitive Europe (European Commission, 2020), among others, the
European  Union  aims  at  ―achieving  climate  neutrality  by  2050  and
decoupling economic growth from resource use‖. In order to ensure a
climate-neutral, circular and resource-efficient economy, the European
Commission will propose policies that can also include references to
environmental taxes – as means of achieving climate neutrality.

According  to  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambitions  (European
Commission, 2020), the greenhouse  gas emissions are to be reduced
of at least 55% by 2030 compared to the year 1990, as it is considered
to improve the wellbeing of EU citizens and to support the COVID-19
recovery,  along  with  the  resilience  and  competitiveness  of  the
European  economy.  In  this  context,  the  EU  taxonomy  will  be  an
essential  instrument  to  bring  finance  closer  to  the  needs  of  the
transition to a cleaner economy. Since it is argued that high levels of
environmental tax revenues can contribute to raising the quality of the
environment  and  environmental  protection  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-
Chudzio,  2017) and  taking  into  consideration  the  importance  for  the
EU  members  to  facilitate  the  transition  to  a  circular  and  climate-
neutral  economy  through  EU  taxonomy,  the  main  objective  of  this
research  was  to  design  a  cross–sectional  linear  regression  model
meant  to  estimate  the  amount  of  environmental  tax  revenues
structurally based on the  amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the
case of EU members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the
year 2018 as the reference point for this study.

Literature review
In  the  European  Union,  the  evolution  of  environmental  tax
revenues is grounded in the historical heritage of each country and it is
influenced by socio-economic aspects such as the degree of economic
development,  size  of  the  population,  consumption  and  production
behaviors and other factors (Štreimikienė, 2015).
Through  environmental  tax  revenues,  the  European  Union
member  states  provide  disincentives  to  consumption  and  build
towards  a  more  green,  environmentally-friendly  economic
development  (Dyduch  and  Stabryła-Chudzio,  2019). European  states
which  have  implemented  reforms  concerning  the  topic  of
environmental  tax  revenues  have  achieved  their  socio-economic  and
environmental  objectives  more  efficiently  than  those  who  did  not
focus,  for  various  reasons,  on  elaborating  and  implementing  well-
thought  environmental  tax  collecting  reforms  (Miceikiene  et  al.,
2016).
However, this is not only the case of the European Union. Fan,
Li  and  Yin  (2019)  mathematically  confirmed  that  imposing

pp. 45  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

environmental  tax  significantly  contributes  to  achieving  green
development, based on a small set of data referring to China. On the
other  hand,  Still,  Piciu,  Ipate  and  Bogdan  (2016)  argue  that
environmental  taxes  should  not  only  act  as  a  tool  for  building  a
cleaner economy, but rather it must also contribute to obtaining a fair
market  price,  in  consonance  with  both  the  results  coming  from  the
economic scientific research teams and from the political will.
Tantau, Maassen and Fratila (2018) designed a panel regression model
meant  to  determine  the  dependency  between  indicators  that  assess
progress  of  the  circular  economy  in  Europe.  In  the  constructed
econometric model, the authors included environmental tax revenues
as  one  of  the  main  independent  variables,  which  proved  to  be
significant  within  the  regression  model  in  relation  to  the  rest  of  the
independent variables and in relation to the dependent variable – the
recycling rate of municipal waste, at the level of the EU-28 members,
corresponding to the 2010-2014 period.
An econometric study carried out at the level of the European
Union level concerning the 2010-2017 period highlights how strategic
and  careful  socio-economic  and  ecological  policies  must  be
constructed,  since  an  increase  of  the  expenses  concerning
environmental  taxes  could  eventually  act  as  an  impediment  for
potential investors in future ecological projects (Banacu et al., 2019),
even  though  taxes  would  initially  be  designed  to  harness  the
implementation of green initiatives.
Through a panel smooth transition regression approach, Cepoi,
Bran  and  Dinu  (2020)  suggest  that  European  countries  should
implement measures designed to avoid environmental degradation by
intensifying the use of biofuels and not only relying on environmental
taxes.
Chu,  Cheng  and  Lai  (2018)  proved  the  importance  of  the
distribution  of  environmental  tax  revenues  per  generations.  They
demonstrated  that  this  form  of  tax  revenues  must  be  considered
according  to  the  needs  and  possibilities  of  both  the  young  and  old
generations. The authors argue that raising environmental taxes could
potentially  generate  inter-generational  conflicts  concerning  the
environmental policy and that would be undesirable considering that
there are ways to appropriately establish thresholds for environmental

[PDF page 6]
taxes in such a manner that can assure the long-term improvement of
welfare of all generations.
Merko,  Dursun  and  Merko  (2018)  demonstrated  that  the
environmental tax revenues represent an important share of Albania’s
GDP  (2.77%  on  average)  and  that  this  form  of  revenues  is
characterized  by  an  average  increase  of  4.7%  in  the  same  analyzed
period, 2008-2015. The greatest share of environmental tax revenues
was registered in the case of the energy sector (56.64%).
In other study, Miceikiene  and Ciuleviciene (2016)  identified
some of the factors that influence the environmental tax revenues and
some  of  those  are  the  following:  nominal  GDP,  energy  saving,
municipality-generated  waste, renewable energy production, nominal
environmental protection expenditure and others. Moreover, the same
authors argue that the nominal GDP has the most impactful influence
on the variation of the environmental tax revenues in Lithuania.
However,  other  authors  (Leibus  and  Mazure,  2016)
demonstrated  that  environmental  tax  revenues  have  relatively  small
shares  in  the  case  of  the  Baltic  States.  Considering  the  1994-2012
timeframe  and  the  European  countries  included  in  the  OECD
database,  a  study  (Onofrei  et  al.,  2017)  based  on  panel  data  fixed-
effect estimation techniques empirically proved that environmental tax
revenues  represent  an  important  vector  designed  to  reduce  pollution
levels,  especially  when  approached  in  relation  to  the  generation  of
greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Speck  (2017)  argues  that  decreasing
greenhouse  gas  emissions  in  the  European  Union  by  80-95%  by  the
year 2050 reported to the 1990 year levels will determine a decrease
of the tax base of both the energy taxes and carbon pricing.

included  in  this  study  are  (i)  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  (ii)
environmental  tax  revenues,  split  per  component  (energy,  transport
and pollution & resources) – as included in Table 1.

The  greenhouse  gas  emissions  indicator  is  part  of  the  EU
Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDG)  designed  to  assess  progress
towards  Goal  13  on  climate  action.  Part  of  the  2030  Agenda  for
Sustainable  Development  (United  Nations,  2015),  SDG  13  aims  to
implement  the  commitment  to  climate  change objectives  and  reduce
the  amount  of  greenhouse  gas  emissions.  Such  measures  are
furthermore  encouraged  by  the  European  Green  Deal,  Circular
Economy  Action  Plan  and  part  of  Europe’s  2030  climate  ambition.
The indicator quantifies total national emissions, international aviation
included. Gases include carbon  dioxide,  methane,  nitrous  oxide,  and
F-gases. Using the individual global warming potential of each of the
gases, they are expressed in units of carbon dioxide equivalents.
As described by Eurostat (2020), environmental  tax revenues
are  part  of  the  environmental  accounts  that  constitute  a  satellite
account  to  national  accounts.  This  indicator  is  split  per  category,  as
described in Table 1. Eurostat considers an environmental tax any tax
whose  base  is  a  physical  unit  of  actions  that  has  a  proven  negative
impact on the natural capital. In order for payments to be identified as
environmental taxes, they must be tracked in the national accounts as
environmental taxes. Other forms of payments to government are not
considered  revenues based on environmental taxes. It is important to

The  research  method  used  in  this  study  is  econometric.
Multiple  cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  designed  in
order  to  find  the  best  model  for  estimating  the  amount  of
environmental tax revenues (i.e.: best tax revenue category), based on
the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  generated  by  the  selected  European
countries included in this study. In all of the constructed econometric
models,  the  greenhouse  gas  emissions  represent  the  independent
variable  and  the  environmental  tax  revenues  (split  per  category)
represent the dependent variable. This research method is quantitative,
based  on  cross–sectional  statistic  data,  characterized  by  multiple
observations studied at a single moment in time (the year 2018 in this
particular  research),  referring  to  multiple  entities  (i.e.:  European
countries).

Conclusion
The  transition  towards  a  greener  circular  economy  with  the
goal  of becoming  climate neutral is made possible, among other, by
resorting  to  an  important  instrument:  environmental  regulations and,
more  specifically,  environmental  tax  revenues.  The  latter  aim  at
mitigating  the  effects  of  harmful  actions  against  the  environment  in
resources-efficient manners, especially in the European Union.
In  the  case  of  the  analyzed  European  countries,  the  energy
sector  represents  the  major  source  of  environmental  pollution  and,
consequently,  a  corresponding  high  level  of  environmental  tax
revenues.  In  2018,  the  governments  of  the  members  part  of  the
European  Union  collected  324.6  billions  €  of  environmental  tax
revenues, representing 2.4% of the European Union’s GDP.
The environment tax proves to be a real policy instrument for
green development. The European Green Deal ensures that taxation is
aligned  with  the  objectives  specific  to  climate  change.  The  2030
Agenda for Sustainable  Development aims at decreasing the  amount
of  greenhouse  gas  emissions  and  this  can  be  made  possible  through
environmental taxes, grounded on the polluter-pays principle.
The main objective of this research was achieved, as multiple
cross–sectional  linear  regression  models  were  constructed  with  the
aim to estimate the amount of environmental tax revenues structurally
based on the amount of greenhouse gas emissions in the case of EU
members plus Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, taking the year 2018
as  the  reference  point  for  this  study. Results  highlight  that  the  only
valid econometric model is that in the case of transport environmental
tax revenues estimated in relation with the generated greenhouse gas
emissions.  The  model  proves  that  one  additional  million  tonne  of

DOI: 10.2478/9788366675261-004
pp. 55  ,  ISSN  | Proceedings of the 7th International Conference ESPERA 2020

[PDF page 15]
greenhouse  gas  emission  implies  additional  taxes,  more  specifically,
14.5451 million EUR of transport environmental taxes, at the level of
the year 2018, in the case of the analyzed European countries.
The  main  limitation  of  this  study  refers  to  the  fact  that  the
analysis does not encompass historic data of the studied phenomena.
However, this study can be extended by approaching the same subject
in  a  different  manner  –  considering  a  panel  data  approach  and  even

Brussels – Environmental tax revenues rose between 2023 and 2024, but as a proportion of GDP they were lower than ten years earlier, [according to data released by Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260722-1), the EU’s statistical office. Environmental tax revenue in the European Union rose to 371.9 billion euros in 2024 from 350.4 billion euros in 2023. This represents a 6.1 per cent increase (+21.4 billion euros). However, “**despite this increase**, **the share of environmental taxes in the EU’s gross domestic product(GDP) declined from 2.5% in 2014 to 2.1% in 2024.**” Furthermore, over the same period, environmental tax revenue as a percentage of total public revenue from taxes and social security contributions fell from 6.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Significant differences remained between the various countries. Bulgaria (9.7 per cent) and Greece (9.4 per cent) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial declines over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7 per cent), Slovenia (7.3 per cent), Latvia (7.2 per cent), and Poland (7 per cent). At the other end, Luxembourg recorded the lowest rate (2.9 per cent), followed by Sweden (3.9 per cent), and Norway (4 per cent). While most countries showed only modest year-on-year changes, significant increases were observed in Italy, where the proportion rose from 5.5 per cent in 2022 to 6.5 per cent in 2024, and in Hungary, from 5.2 per cent in 2022 to 5.8 per cent in 2024. “Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at the EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe,” Eurostat said. More specifically, energy taxes accounted for over three-quarters (77.2 per cent) of total environmental tax revenue in the EU, reaching 287 billion euros in 2024 from 269.3 billion euros the previous year. Transport taxes (18 per cent of the total) amounted to 67 billion euros in 2024 compared with 64 billion euros in 2023, while taxes on pollution and resources (4.8 per cent) totalled 17.9 billion euros compared with €17.2 billion in 2023. The figures show that environmental tax revenue increased in 22 EU countries in 2024. Romania recorded the highest growth (+21.7 per cent), followed by Lithuania and Poland, with 13.9 per cent and 12.7 per cent, respectively. Hungary (+12.2 per cent) and Poland (+11.2 per cent) are also among the countries with the highest increases. Brussels – Environmental tax revenues rose between 2023 and 2024, but as a proportion of GDP they were lower than ten years earlier, [according to data released by Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20260722-1), the EU’s statistical office. Environmental tax revenue in the European Union rose to 371.9 billion euros in 2024 from 350.4 billion euros in 2023. This represents a 6.1 per cent increase (+21.4 billion euros). However, “**despite this increase**, **the share of environmental taxes in the EU’s gross domestic product(GDP) declined from 2.5% in 2014 to 2.1% in 2024.**” Furthermore, over the same period, environmental tax revenue as a percentage of total public revenue from taxes and social security contributions fell from 6.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent. Significant differences remained between the various countries. Bulgaria (9.7 per cent) and Greece (9.4 per cent) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial declines over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7 per cent), Slovenia (7.3 per cent), Latvia (7.2 per cent), and Poland (7 per cent). At the other end, Luxembourg recorded the lowest rate (2.9 per cent), followed by Sweden (3.9 per cent), and Norway (4 per cent). While most countries showed only modest year-on-year changes, significant increases were observed in Italy, where the proportion rose from 5.5 per cent in 2022 to 6.5 per cent in 2024, and in Hungary, from 5.2 per cent in 2022 to 5.8 per cent in 2024. “Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at the EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe,” Eurostat said. More specifically, energy taxes accounted for over three-quarters (77.2 per cent) of total environmental tax revenue in the EU, reaching 287 billion euros in 2024 from 269.3 billion euros the previous year. Transport taxes (18 per cent of the total) amounted to 67 billion euros in 2024 compared with 64 billion euros in 2023, while taxes on pollution and resources (4.8 per cent) totalled 17.9 billion euros compared with €17.2 billion in 2023. The figures show that environmental tax revenue increased in 22 EU countries in 2024. Romania recorded the highest growth (+21.7 per cent), followed by Lithuania and Poland, with 13.9 per cent and 12.7 per cent, respectively. Hungary (+12.2 per cent) and Poland (+11.2 per cent) are also among the countries with the highest increases. In five EU countries,revenues fell compared with the previous year: Sweden (-17.7 per cent), Slovakia (-6.1 per cent), Finland (-3.8 per cent), Greece (-3.7 per cent), and Bulgaria (-2.3 per cent). _English version by the [Translation Service of Withub](https://www.withub.it/en/translate/)_ Tags:[environment](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/environment-en/)[eurostat](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/eurostat-en-2/)[fees](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/cup-in/)[gettito fiscale ambientale](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/gettito-fiscale-ambientale/)[pil](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/pills/)[ue](https://www.eunews.it/en/tag/ue/) ### Eunews Newsletter MORNING - [x] From Tuesday to Friday, the day’s top stories straight to your inbox. # Environmental Taxes

**5** Indicators | **1995 - 2021** |**125** Economies (Updated: **over 1 year ago**)

Source: [International Monetary Fund (IMF)](https://www.imf.org/)

This dataset demonstrates how governments are responding to climate change through taxation and spending based on official statistics and implicit and explicit fossil fuel subsidies based on model-based estimates. It focuses particularly on government revenues from environmental taxes on energy, transport, pollution and resource consumption.  
  
Details on the methodology are available at **[https://climatedata.imf.org/datasets/3fb1ed30d3394574b3145246846023b1_0/about](https://climatedata.imf.org/datasets/3fb1ed30d3394574b3145246846023b1_0/about)**

# Environmental Taxes

**5** Indicators | **1995 - 2021** |**125** Economies (Updated: **over 1 year ago**)

Source: [International Monetary Fund (IMF)](https://www.imf.org/)

This dataset demonstrates how governments are responding to climate change through taxation and spending based on official statistics and implicit and explicit fossil fuel subsidies based on model-based estimates. It focuses particularly on government revenues from environmental taxes on energy, transport, pollution and resource consumption.  
  
Details on the methodology are available at **[https://climatedata.imf.org/datasets/3fb1ed30d3394574b3145246846023b1_0/about](https://climatedata.imf.org/datasets/3fb1ed30d3394574b3145246846023b1_0/about)**

## Summary

A tax whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific, negative impact on the environment.

These are subdivided into four types of taxes: taxes on energy (including fuel for transport); taxes on transport (excluding fuel for transport), taxes on pollution and taxes on resources.

  

**Sources:**Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (2020), Environmentally Related Tax Revenue, OECD.Stat[https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=ERTR](https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=ERTR). Accessed on 2023-06-17; International Monetary Fund (IMF), Statistics Department (Government Finance Division) Questionnaire.  

  

**Category:****Mitigation**  

  

**Data series:**

*   Environmental Taxes
*   Taxes on Energy (including fuel for transport)
*   Taxes on Pollution
*   Taxes on Resources
*   Taxes on Transport (excluding fuel for transport)

**Methodology:**  

  

Environmental taxes are a subset of taxes, as defined in the 2008 System of National Accounts and the Government Finance Statistics Manual 2014, whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific, negative impact on the environment.

# Europe's Leaders In Environmental Taxation

by[Niall McCarthy](mailto:), 

 Feb 20, 2020 

 The European Union 

Eurostat has released [new data](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/-/DDN-20200219-1/?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=/eurostat/en/news/whats-new) showing that environmental tax revenue across the [European Union](https://www.statista.com/topics/921/european-union/) totalled €324.6 billion in 2018, a 3 percent increase on the previous year. That total is also 49 percent higher than in 2002 and it mainly consists of energy taxes (77.7 percent), followed by transport taxes (19.1 percent) and pollution and resource taxes (3.3 percent).

Environmental taxes as a share of total taxes & social contributions were highest in Latvia in 2018 at 10.9 percent, followed by Bulgaria with 9.8 percent and Greece with 9.5 percent. The lowest shares were seen in Luxembourg at 4.4 percent and Germany at 4.5 percent. The Eurostat data also showed taxes in several non-EU nations. Environmental taxes accounted for 7 percent of the [UK's total tax revenue](https://www.statista.com/topics/3834/tax-in-the-uk/) along with 6.2 percent of Switzerland's and 5.5 percent of Norway's.

# Europe's Leaders In Environmental Taxation

by[Niall McCarthy](mailto:), 

 Feb 20, 2020 

 The European Union 

Eurostat has released [new data](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/-/DDN-20200219-1/?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=/eurostat/en/news/whats-new) showing that environmental tax revenue across the [European Union](https://www.statista.com/topics/921/european-union/) totalled €324.6 billion in 2018, a 3 percent increase on the previous year. That total is also 49 percent higher than in 2002 and it mainly consists of energy taxes (77.7 percent), followed by transport taxes (19.1 percent) and pollution and resource taxes (3.3 percent).

Environmental taxes as a share of total taxes & social contributions were highest in Latvia in 2018 at 10.9 percent, followed by Bulgaria with 9.8 percent and Greece with 9.5 percent. The lowest shares were seen in Luxembourg at 4.4 percent and Germany at 4.5 percent. The Eurostat data also showed taxes in several non-EU nations. Environmental taxes accounted for 7 percent of the [UK's total tax revenue](https://www.statista.com/topics/3834/tax-in-the-uk/) along with 6.2 percent of Switzerland's and 5.5 percent of Norway's.

## International Tax Competitiveness Index

The Tax Foundation' s _[International Tax Competitiveness Index (ITCI)](https://taxfoundation.org/publications/international-tax-competitiveness-index/)_ measures the degree to which the 38 OECD countries' tax systems promote competitiveness through low tax burdens on business investment and neutrality through a well-structured tax code. The _ITCI_ considers more than 40 variables across five categories: Corporate Taxes, Individual Taxes, Consumption Taxes, Property Taxes, and International Tax Rules.

The _ITCI_ attempts to display not only which countries provide the best tax environment for investment but also the best tax environment for workers and businesses.

## Sources of Revenue in Denmark

Countries raise tax revenue through a mix of individual income taxes, corporate income taxes, social insurance taxes, taxes on goods and services, and property taxes. The mix of tax policies can influence how distortionary or neutral a tax system is. Taxes on income can create more economic harm than taxes on consumption and property. However, the extent to which an individual country relies on any of these taxes can differ substantially.

## Corporate Taxation in Denmark

The corporate income tax is a tax on the profits of corporations. All OECD countries levy a tax on corporate profits, but the rates and bases vary widely from country to country. Corporate income taxes are the most harmful tax for economic growth, but countries can mitigate those harms with lower corporate tax rates and generous capital allowances.

Capital allowances directly impact business incentives for new investments. In most countries, businesses are generally not allowed to immediately deduct the cost of capital investments. Instead, they are required to deduct these costs over several years, increasing the tax burden on new investments. This can be measured by calculating the percent of the present value cost that a business can deduct over the life of an asset. Countries with more generous capital allowances have tax systems that are more supportive to business investment, which underpins economic growth.

## Individual Taxation in Denmark

Individual taxes are one of the most prevalent means of raising revenue to fund government across the OECD. Individual income taxes are levied on an individual's or household's income to fund general government operations. These taxes are typically progressive, meaning that the rate at which an individual's income is taxed increases as the individual earns more income.

In addition, countries have payroll taxes. These typically flat-rate taxes are levied on wage income in addition to a country's general individual income tax. However, revenue from these taxes is typically allocated specifically toward social insurance programs such as unemployment insurance, government pension programs, and health insurance.

High marginal income tax rates impact decisions to work and reduce the efficiency with which governments can raise revenue from their individual tax systems.

Capital gains and dividend income—if not included in the individual income tax—are typically taxed at a flat rate.

## Consumption Taxes in Denmark

Consumption taxes are charged on goods and services and can take various forms. In the OECD and most of the world, the value-added tax (VAT) is the most common consumption tax. Most consumption taxes either do not tax intermediate business inputs or provide a credit for taxes already paid on inputs, which avoids the problem of tax pyramiding, whereby the same final good or service is taxed multiple times in the production process. The exclusion of business inputs makes a consumption tax one of the most economically efficient means of raising tax revenue.

However, many countries fail to define their tax base correctly. To minimize distortions, all final consumption should be taxed at the same standard rate. However, countries often exempt too many goods and services from taxation or tax them at reduced rates, which requires them to levy higher standard rates to raise sufficient revenue. Some countries also fail to properly exempt business inputs. For example, states in the United States often levy sales taxes on machinery and equipment.

## Property Taxes in Denmark

Property taxes apply to assets of an individual or a business. Estate and inheritance taxes, for example, are due upon the death of an individual and the passing of his or her estate to an heir, respectively. Taxes on real property, on the other hand, are paid at set intervals—often annually—on the value of taxable property such as land and houses.

Many property taxes are highly distortive and add significant complexity to the life of a taxpayer or business. Estate and inheritance taxes create disincentives against additional work and saving, which damages productivity and output. Financial transaction taxes increase the cost of capital, which limits the flow of investment capital to its most efficient allocations. Taxes on wealth limit the capital available in the economy, which damages long-term economic growth and innovation.

Sound tax policy minimizes economic distortions. With the exception of taxes on land, most property taxes increase economic distortions and have long-term negative effects on an economy and its productivity.

## International Taxes in Denmark

In an increasingly globalized economy, businesses often expand beyond the borders of their home countries to reach customers around the world. As a result, countries need to define rules determining how, or if, corporate income earned in foreign countries is taxed. International tax rules deal with the systems and regulations that countries apply to those business activities.

Tax treaties align many tax laws between two countries and attempt to reduce double taxation, particularly by reducing or eliminating withholding taxes between the countries. Countries with a greater number of partners in their tax treaty network have more attractive tax regimes for foreign investment and are more competitive than countries with fewer treaties.
